obligations.name: Federal corporate income tax return
obligations.action: File Form 1120 and pay any tax due, or file Form 7004 for a six month extension to file (not to pay).
obligations.penalty: 5% of the unpaid tax for each month late, up to 25%, plus interest
obligations.explanation: A C corporation files its own income tax return on Form 1120 by the 15th day of the fourth month after its fiscal year ends, which is April 15 for a calendar year. An extension on Form 7004 gives six more months to file, but the tax itself is still due on the original date.

obligations.name: Federal S corporation return
obligations.action: File Form 1120-S and give each shareholder a Schedule K-1, or file Form 7004 for a six month extension.
obligations.penalty: $255 per shareholder for each month late, up to 12 months (the 2026 figure, adjusted yearly)
obligations.explanation: An S corporation files Form 1120-S by the 15th day of the third month after its fiscal year ends, March 15 for a calendar year. The return itself owes no tax in most cases, but the late filing penalty is charged per shareholder per month, so a late return with three owners costs more than most people expect.

obligations.name: Federal partnership return
obligations.action: File Form 1065 and give each partner or member a Schedule K-1, or file Form 7004 for a six month extension.
obligations.penalty: $255 per partner for each month late, up to 12 months (the 2026 figure, adjusted yearly)
obligations.explanation: A partnership, including a multi member LLC that has not elected corporate treatment, files Form 1065 by the 15th day of the third month after its year ends. The partners report their shares on their own returns from the K-1s, so this return has to be done before anyone's personal return can be.

obligations.name: Business income on the owner's personal return
obligations.form: Form 1040, Schedule C and Schedule SE
obligations.action: Report the business on Schedule C with the owner's Form 1040 and pay self employment tax on Schedule SE, or file Form 4868 for a six month extension.
obligations.penalty: 5% of the unpaid tax for each month late, up to 25%, plus interest
obligations.explanation: A sole proprietorship or single member LLC has no return of its own. Its income and expenses go on Schedule C with the owner's personal return, due April 15, and the owner pays self employment tax on the net profit through Schedule SE. An LLC owned by a person outside the United States is different: see the nonresident owner's return.

obligations.name: Nonresident owner's US return, if one is owed
obligations.action: If the LLC carried on a trade or business in the United States, its owner files Form 1040-NR reporting the income effectively connected with it, by June 15 (April 15 if the owner also had US wages). An LLC with no US trade or business, such as one that only holds assets or sells services performed abroad, files no income tax return; Form 5472 with its pro forma Form 1120 still goes in.
obligations.penalty: 5% of the unpaid tax for each month late, up to 25%, plus interest, when a return is owed
obligations.explanation: A single member LLC owned by someone who is not a US person is disregarded for income tax, so the question is whether the owner has US tax to report. If the LLC runs a trade or business in the United States, income effectively connected with it goes on the owner's Form 1040-NR, due June 15 for an owner with no US wages, and the owner pays no self employment tax unless a totalization agreement says otherwise. If the LLC has no US trade or business, which is the common case for a holding LLC or for services performed from abroad, there is no income tax return at all, only the Form 5472 information return and, with foreign accounts, the FBAR. The owner's Form 1040-ES estimates are not on this calendar because they only arise once there is a US return; a tax adviser can confirm which side of the line the LLC falls on.

obligations.name: Annual electronic notice for small exempt organizations
obligations.action: File Form 990-N online through the IRS e-Postcard system. It takes ten minutes, there is no extension and no penalty; three consecutive missed years revoke the exemption automatically.
obligations.penalty: No monetary penalty, but an organization that misses three years in a row loses its exemption automatically
obligations.explanation: An exempt organization whose gross receipts are normally $50,000 or less files the e-Postcard instead of a full return, by the 15th day of the fifth month after its fiscal year ends, May 15 for a calendar year. It asks for eight pieces of information and nothing financial. The danger is not the penalty, there is none, but automatic revocation: three consecutive missed filings and the exemption is gone, with reinstatement costing a new application and a fee.

obligations.name: Short annual return of an exempt organization
obligations.action: File Form 990-EZ electronically, with Schedule A for a public charity, or file Form 8868 for an automatic six month extension.
obligations.penalty: $25 a day, up to the lesser of $13,000 or 5% of gross receipts (returns filed in 2026; adjusted yearly); automatic loss of exemption after three missed years
obligations.explanation: An exempt organization with gross receipts under $200,000 and total assets under $500,000 may file the short form, Form 990-EZ, by the 15th day of the fifth month after its fiscal year ends. A public charity attaches Schedule A, which carries the public support test. Form 8868 extends the filing date by six months automatically. The return is public: donors, funders and the press read it, so it is worth filing well.

obligations.name: Annual return of an exempt organization
obligations.action: File Form 990 electronically with its schedules, or file Form 8868 for an automatic six month extension. Have the board review it before it goes.
obligations.penalty: $25 a day, up to the lesser of $13,000 or 5% of gross receipts ($130 a day up to $65,000 for organizations with gross receipts over $1,309,500); the figures are for returns filed in 2026 and are adjusted yearly; automatic loss of exemption after three missed years
obligations.explanation: An exempt organization with gross receipts of $200,000 or more, or total assets of $500,000 or more, files the full Form 990 by the 15th day of the fifth month after its fiscal year ends, May 15 for a calendar year. It is an information return rather than a tax return, but it is the most read document a nonprofit produces: it is public, it carries the governance questions, the compensation of officers and the public support test. Form 8868 gives an automatic six month extension; the penalty for a late return runs by the day.

obligations.name: Annual return of a private foundation
obligations.action: File Form 990-PF electronically and pay the excise tax on net investment income, or file Form 8868 for an automatic six month extension.
obligations.penalty: $25 a day, up to the lesser of $13,000 or 5% of gross receipts (returns filed in 2026; adjusted yearly); 5% a month on unpaid excise tax; automatic loss of exemption after three missed years
obligations.explanation: Every private foundation files Form 990-PF, whatever its size, by the 15th day of the fifth month after its fiscal year ends. The return reports the 1.39% excise tax on net investment income and shows whether the foundation met its minimum distribution requirement, roughly 5% of the value of its investment assets each year. A foundation that expects to owe $500 or more in excise tax also pays estimated tax in quarterly installments on the same dates as a corporation.

obligations.name: Exempt organization business income tax return
obligations.action: File Form 990-T and pay the tax on unrelated business income, or file Form 8868 for an automatic six month extension. Pay estimated tax during the year if the tax will be $500 or more.
obligations.penalty: 5% of the unpaid tax for each month late, up to 25%, plus interest
obligations.explanation: Income from a trade or business that is regularly carried on and unrelated to the exempt purpose is taxed like corporate income. Once gross income from it reaches $1,000 in a year, the organization files Form 990-T by the 15th day of the fifth month after its fiscal year ends, alongside the Form 990, and pays the tax at the corporate rate. Each unrelated business is computed separately. If the tax will be $500 or more, quarterly estimated payments are due as for a corporation.

obligations.name: Written acknowledgments to donors
obligations.action: Send every donor who gave $250 or more in the previous year a written acknowledgment stating the amount, whether any goods or services were provided in return, and their value.
obligations.penalty: The donor loses the deduction; the organization owes $10 per disclosure, up to $5,000 per event, for failing to disclose quid pro quo contributions over $75
obligations.explanation: A donor cannot deduct a gift of $250 or more without a written acknowledgment from the charity, received before the donor files their return. The law sets no date for the charity, but January 31 is the working deadline that keeps every donor's return on time, and it matches the W-2 and 1099 season. The acknowledgment names the amount, says whether the donor received anything in return, and values it if so. Gifts over $75 made partly in exchange for goods or services need the disclosure at the time of the gift.

obligations.name: Corporate estimated tax payment
obligations.form: Estimated tax worksheet in the Form 1120 instructions, paid through EFTPS
obligations.action: Pay the quarterly installment through EFTPS if the corporation expects to owe $500 or more for the year.
obligations.penalty: An underpayment penalty computed on Form 2220, charged as interest for each day the installment is short
obligations.explanation: A C corporation that expects to owe $500 or more pays its income tax in four installments during the year, on the 15th day of the fourth, sixth, ninth and twelfth months of its fiscal year. For a calendar year that is April 15, June 15, September 15 and December 15; a June 30 fiscal year pays October 15, December 15, March 15 and June 15. The dates here follow the fiscal year you gave.

obligations.name: Owners' estimated tax payments
obligations.action: Each owner pays estimated tax on their share of the business income if they expect to owe $1,000 or more after withholding.
obligations.penalty: An underpayment penalty computed on Form 2210, charged as interest on each short installment
obligations.explanation: Income from an S corporation or a partnership is taxed on the owners' personal returns, and the IRS wants that tax paid during the year. Owners who expect to owe $1,000 or more pay in four installments: April 15, June 15, September 15 and January 15 of the following year. Withholding from a salary counts toward the total, which is why many S corporation owners cover it through their own paychecks instead.

obligations.name: Owner's estimated tax payment
obligations.action: Pay estimated income and self employment tax on the business profit if you expect to owe $1,000 or more for the year after any withholding.
obligations.penalty: An underpayment penalty computed on Form 2210, charged as interest on each short installment
obligations.explanation: A sole proprietor or single member LLC owner pays income tax and self employment tax on the business profit through their own return, and the IRS wants it paid during the year. An owner who expects to owe $1,000 or more pays in four installments: April 15, June 15, September 15 and January 15 of the following year. Withholding from a job or a spouse's salary counts toward the total.

obligations.name: Quarterly federal payroll tax return
obligations.action: File Form 941 reporting wages, federal income tax withheld and both halves of Social Security and Medicare tax for the quarter.
obligations.penalty: 5% of the unpaid tax for each month late, up to 25%, plus failure to deposit penalties of 2% to 15%
obligations.explanation: Nearly every employer files Form 941 four times a year, by the last day of the month after each quarter: April 30, July 31, October 31 and January 31. It reconciles what was withheld from employees and what the employer owes in Social Security and Medicare tax against the deposits already made. The smallest employers, those the IRS has told to file Form 944 because their annual liability is $1,000 or less, file once a year by January 31 instead. A payroll provider normally files it; the company is still the one liable.

obligations.name: Federal payroll tax deposit
obligations.action: Deposit the previous month's withheld income tax and Social Security and Medicare tax through EFTPS. Semiweekly depositors deposit within days of each payday instead.
obligations.penalty: 2% if up to 5 days late, 5% up to 15 days, 10% beyond that, 15% after an IRS notice
obligations.explanation: The tax withheld from paychecks belongs to the government the moment it is withheld, and the IRS wants it deposited on a schedule. A monthly schedule depositor, which covers most employers with under $50,000 in annual payroll tax, deposits by the 15th of the following month. Larger employers deposit semiweekly: by the following Wednesday for a Wednesday, Thursday or Friday payday, and by the following Friday for a Saturday through Tuesday payday. If a payroll provider handles your payroll, it makes these deposits and you can mark this line as handled.

obligations.name: Annual federal unemployment tax return
obligations.action: File Form 940 and pay any FUTA tax still owed for the previous year.
obligations.penalty: 5% of the unpaid tax for each month late, up to 25%
obligations.explanation: Federal unemployment tax is an employer only tax of 6% on the first $7,000 paid to each employee, reduced to 0.6% for employers that pay state unemployment tax on time. Form 940 reports it once a year, by January 31. Quarterly deposits are due during the year once the liability passes $500. An organization exempt under section 501(c)(3) owes no federal unemployment tax and files no Form 940; other exempt organizations, such as 501(c)(4) and 501(c)(6) groups, do.

obligations.name: Federal unemployment tax deposit
obligations.action: Deposit the federal unemployment tax through EFTPS if the amount owed for the year so far has passed $500; below that it carries over to the next quarter, or to Form 940 in January.
obligations.penalty: Failure to deposit penalties of 2% to 15%, as for payroll tax deposits
obligations.explanation: The unemployment tax reported on Form 940 is deposited during the year, by the last day of the month after each quarter, whenever the tax owed so far passes $500: April 30, July 31, October 31 and January 31. At 0.6% of the first $7,000 per employee, that is $42 an employee a year, so an employer with a dozen people deposits once or twice a year and pays the rest with the return. A payroll provider makes the deposits for its clients; this line is for companies running their own payroll.

obligations.name: W-2 forms to employees and the SSA
obligations.action: Give every employee a W-2 for the previous year and file copies with the Social Security Administration with the W-3 transmittal.
obligations.penalty: $60 to $340 per form depending on how late (the figures for forms due in 2026, adjusted yearly), with no cap for intentional disregard
obligations.explanation: Employees need their W-2 to file their own taxes, so the deadline is early: January 31, both for the copy to the employee and the copy to the Social Security Administration. Penalties are per form and grow the longer the forms are late. Payroll providers prepare and file these as part of year end.

obligations.name: 1099-NEC forms to contractors and the IRS
obligations.action: Send a 1099-NEC to every US contractor paid $2,000 or more in the previous year and file the copies with the IRS. Collect a W-9 from each contractor before you pay them.
obligations.penalty: $60 to $340 per form depending on how late (the figures for forms due in 2026, adjusted yearly), with no cap for intentional disregard
obligations.explanation: Payments of $2,000 or more in a year to an individual or unincorporated business for services are reported on Form 1099-NEC by January 31, to the contractor and to the IRS. The threshold rose from $600 to $2,000 for payments made from January 1, 2026, so the forms due January 31, 2027 are the first at the new figure, which is indexed for inflation after 2026. Payments to corporations are mostly exempt, which is why a W-9 on file for every contractor matters: it tells you who needs a form. Ten or more information returns in a year must be filed electronically. Rent paid to an individual or an LLC landlord goes on the cousin form, 1099-MISC, on the same date and at the same $2,000 threshold.

obligations.name: Report of foreign bank and financial accounts
obligations.action: File the FBAR electronically through FinCEN's BSA E-Filing System for every foreign account the company held, owned or had signature authority over, if their combined value passed $10,000 at any time in the previous year. Missed April 15? The extension to October 15 is automatic.
obligations.penalty: Up to about $16,500 per non willful violation (the 2025 figure, adjusted yearly); the greater of about $165,000 or 50% of the account balance if willful
obligations.explanation: A US company with a bank, brokerage or mobile money account outside the United States reports it to FinCEN every year on the FBAR when the combined value of all foreign accounts passed $10,000 at any point in the year, even for a day. It is not a tax form and it goes to FinCEN, not the IRS, by April 15, with an automatic extension to October 15 that needs no request. Officers who can sign on the account have their own filing to make. The penalties are the harshest in this calendar for a form that takes twenty minutes, which is why it stays on the list for any company with money abroad.

obligations.name: Information return of a foreign owned company
obligations.form: Form 5472 (with Form 1120, or a pro forma Form 1120 for a disregarded LLC)
obligations.action: File Form 5472 with the corporation's Form 1120, or with a pro forma Form 1120 for a single member LLC owned by a non US person, reporting the transactions with the foreign owner. Form 7004 extends it with the return.
obligations.penalty: $25,000 per form, plus $25,000 for each 30 day period that the failure continues beyond 90 days after an IRS notice
obligations.explanation: A US corporation that is 25% or more foreign owned, and since 2017 any single member LLC owned by a non US person, reports its dealings with that owner every year on Form 5472: capital contributions, loans, payments, anything that moved between them. The LLC version catches people out because the LLC files no income tax return of its own; it still attaches Form 5472 to a cover Form 1120 by the 15th day of the fourth month after the year ends. The penalty is $25,000 whether the form is late or missing, and the IRS applies it.

obligations.name: Partnership withholding on foreign partners
obligations.action: File Form 8804 with a Form 8805 for each foreign partner, reporting the tax withheld on their share of the partnership's US business income, by the 15th day of the third month after the year ends; pay the withholding in installments on Form 8813 during the year.
obligations.penalty: 5% of the unpaid tax for each month late, up to 25%, plus a penalty per missing Form 8805
obligations.explanation: A partnership, or an LLC taxed as one, with a partner who is not a US person withholds tax on that partner's share of the income connected with a US business, at the top rate, and pays it in quarterly installments on Form 8813. After year end it files Form 8804 with a Form 8805 for each foreign partner, by the same date as Form 1065. The foreign partner uses the 8805 to claim the credit on their own US return.

obligations.name: Information return on a foreign company the company owns (corporations)
obligations.action: File Form 5471 with the income tax return for each foreign corporation in which the company holds 10% or more, with the schedules its category of filer requires. The extension of the return extends it.
obligations.penalty: $10,000 per form per year, plus $10,000 for each month after an IRS notice, up to $50,000 more, and a reduction of foreign tax credits
obligations.explanation: A US company that owns 10% or more of a company organized outside the United States, a subsidiary in Ghana or a joint venture in Kenya for instance, reports it every year on Form 5471, attached to its own income tax return. The form asks for the foreign company's balance sheet, income statement and transactions with the US owner. It is long, the categories of filer are confusing, and the penalty is $10,000 per form whether or not any tax is due, so it belongs on the calendar beside the return it travels with.

obligations.name: Information return on a foreign company the company owns (S corporations and partnerships)
obligations.action: File Form 5471 with Form 1120-S or Form 1065 for each foreign corporation in which the company holds 10% or more, with the schedules its category of filer requires. The extension of the return extends it.
obligations.penalty: $10,000 per form per year, plus $10,000 for each month after an IRS notice, up to $50,000 more
obligations.explanation: An S corporation or partnership that owns 10% or more of a company organized outside the United States reports it every year on Form 5471, attached to its own return by the 15th day of the third month after the year ends. The form asks for the foreign company's balance sheet, income statement and transactions with the US owner, and the penalty is $10,000 per form whether or not any tax is due.

obligations.name: Withholding returns for payments to foreign persons
obligations.action: File Form 1042 and a Form 1042-S for each foreign person paid US source income in the previous year (royalties, interest, dividends, services performed in the United States), and give each payee their copy. Keep a Form W-8BEN or W-8BEN-E on file for every foreign payee before you pay them.
obligations.penalty: $60 to $340 per form for late or missing 1042-S forms (the figures for forms due in 2026, adjusted yearly); 5% a month on unpaid withholding, up to 25%, and personal liability for tax that should have been withheld
obligations.explanation: Paying people and companies outside the United States is simpler than most owners fear, with one rule at the center: income is reported and withheld on only when it is US source. A developer in Lagos or Manila paid for work done there is foreign source and needs no 1042-S, only a W-8BEN on file to prove it. Royalties, interest, dividends and services performed on US soil are US source, taxed at 30% unless a treaty lowers it, and reported on Form 1042-S by March 15 with the Form 1042 summary. The W-8 forms are the whole defense if the IRS asks why nothing was withheld, so collecting them is the part to do every time.

obligations.name: Annual meeting of shareholders and directors
obligations.agency: The company's own bylaws and its state's corporation law
obligations.action: Hold the annual meeting of shareholders to elect directors and the directors' meeting to appoint officers, or sign written consents in place of each, and keep the minutes with the company's records. Pick a month and keep it.
obligations.explanation: Every state's corporation law requires an annual meeting of shareholders, Delaware's in section 211, and the bylaws usually set the month. A one person corporation satisfies it with a signed written consent. Nothing is filed and no agency checks, which is why it slips, and why it matters later: a lender, an investor or a buyer asks for the minute book, and a corporation that cannot show its meetings looks like a corporation that did not keep its form. It has no fixed date here; choose one and add it as your own date with annual recurrence.

obligations.name: Annual meeting of the board
obligations.agency: The organization's own bylaws and its state's nonprofit corporation law
obligations.action: Hold the board meeting the bylaws require, at least once a year, elect officers and any directors whose terms end, approve the budget, review the Form 990 before it is filed, and keep the minutes.
obligations.explanation: A nonprofit's board meets as its bylaws say, at least once a year under every state's nonprofit corporation law, and the Form 990 asks whether the board reviewed the return before it was filed and whether the minutes were kept. Funders read those answers. There is no fixed date; choose the month your bylaws set and add it as your own date with annual recurrence.

obligations.name: Annual retirement plan return
obligations.action: File Form 5500 (or 5500-SF for small plans) for the plan year through the EFAST2 system, or file Form 5558 for an extension.
obligations.penalty: Up to $2,739 a day from the Department of Labor, plus IRS penalties
obligations.explanation: Employer retirement plans under ERISA file an annual return seven months after the plan year ends, July 31 for a calendar year plan. Many plan providers prepare it, but the plan sponsor signs and is liable. A one participant plan with under $250,000 in assets may be exempt; a SEP or SIMPLE IRA generally has no Form 5500 at all.

obligations.name: Summary annual report to plan participants
obligations.action: Give every plan participant the summary annual report, a one page digest of the Form 5500, within nine months after the plan year ends, or two months after an extended Form 5500 is filed.
obligations.penalty: Up to $110 a day per participant who asked for it and did not get it, under ERISA's disclosure rules
obligations.explanation: Every plan that files a Form 5500 also tells its participants what was in it, through the summary annual report, within nine months after the plan year ends, September 30 for a calendar year plan, or two months after the extended filing date if the Form 5500 was extended. Plan providers usually prepare it from the return; the sponsor distributes it, on paper or electronically under the Department of Labor's rules. Plans exempt from the Form 5500 have no summary to give.

obligations.name: Health coverage statements to employees
obligations.action: Give each full time employee a Form 1095-C for the previous year, or post a notice that the form is available on request where the law allows.
obligations.penalty: $60 to $340 per form
obligations.explanation: An employer with 50 or more full time equivalent employees is an applicable large employer under the Affordable Care Act. It reports the health coverage it offered on Form 1095-C: a copy to each full time employee by March 2, and the set to the IRS with Form 1094-C by March 31 when filed electronically. The employer mandate penalty applies when coverage is not offered to 95% of full time staff.

obligations.name: Health coverage returns to the IRS
obligations.action: File Forms 1094-C and 1095-C electronically with the IRS.
obligations.penalty: $60 to $340 per form
obligations.explanation: The IRS copy of the health coverage reporting is due March 31 for electronic filers, which covers almost every employer since the ten return threshold for mandatory electronic filing.

obligations.name: Post the OSHA injury and illness summary
obligations.action: Post the previous year's Form 300A summary in the workplace from February 1 to April 30, signed by a company executive, unless your industry is on OSHA's partially exempt list.
obligations.penalty: Up to $16,550 per violation
obligations.explanation: Employers with more than ten employees keep an OSHA 300 log of work related injuries and illnesses, unless their industry is on OSHA's list of low hazard industries, which covers most offices, retail and professional services. The annual summary (Form 300A) is posted where employees can see it from February 1 through April 30, even when there were no cases.

obligations.name: Submit injury and illness data to OSHA
obligations.action: Submit Form 300A data through OSHA's Injury Tracking Application if the establishment has 20 or more employees and is in a designated high hazard industry, or 250 or more employees in any industry that keeps records.
obligations.penalty: Up to $16,550 per violation
obligations.explanation: Beyond posting the summary, some employers submit it electronically by March 2: establishments with 20 to 249 employees in industries on OSHA's designated list, and establishments with 100 or more employees in those industries also submit the detailed 300 and 301 data. If your industry is not on the list and you have fewer than 250 employees, this does not apply.

obligations.name: EEO-1 workforce demographics report

schedule.note: The EEOC sets the collection window each year, usually opening in spring with a deadline in late spring or early summer.

obligations.action: File the EEO-1 Component 1 report through the EEOC's online portal during the annual collection window.
obligations.penalty: Court ordered compliance; repeated failure can bar federal contracts
obligations.explanation: Private employers with 100 or more employees, and federal contractors with 50 or more, report their workforce by job category, sex, race and ethnicity each year. The EEOC announces the window annually, so the date shown is typical rather than fixed. Jay updates it when the EEOC publishes the year's deadline.

obligations.name: New hire reporting
obligations.action: Report every new or rehired employee to the state new hire directory within 20 days of the start date (sooner in some states). A payroll provider normally does it with the first payroll.
obligations.penalty: Up to $25 per unreported employee in most states, $500 when the failure is a conspiracy with the employee
obligations.explanation: Federal law requires every employer to report new and rehired employees to its state within 20 days, so child support orders can be enforced. It is an event, not a date, which is why it lives here rather than on a calendar day. Payroll providers file it automatically; an employer that runs its own payroll files online with the state directory.

obligations.name: Form I-9 for every employee
obligations.action: Complete Form I-9 for each new employee within three business days of the start date, with the documents it lists, and keep it for three years after hire or one year after the employee leaves, whichever is later. Keep a tickler for work authorizations that expire.
obligations.penalty: $288 to $2,861 per form for paperwork violations, more for knowingly employing someone not authorized to work
obligations.explanation: Every US employer verifies each employee's identity and authorization to work on Form I-9, within three business days of the first day of work. Nothing is filed; the forms are kept and produced on inspection, and the fines are per form, so a company with sloppy files pays for each one. Reverify when a work authorization document expires.

obligations.name: Workers' compensation insurance
obligations.form: An insurance policy or a state fund account
obligations.action: Keep a workers' compensation policy in force in every state where you have employees, from the first employee in most states, and give the policy renewal date to your calendar as your own date.
obligations.penalty: State fines that run from hundreds to thousands of dollars a day, stop work orders, and personal liability for an injured employee's costs
obligations.explanation: Nearly every state requires an employer to carry workers' compensation insurance from its first employee (Texas makes it optional, and a few states start at three to five employees). The policy comes from an insurer or, in Ohio, North Dakota, Washington and Wyoming, from the state fund. The state checks against payroll filings, and an uninsured employer is fined by the day. The renewal date is the insurer's, so add it as your own date.

obligations.name: Workplace posters
obligations.agency: Department of Labor and your state labor agency
obligations.form: Federal and state labor law posters
obligations.action: Display the current federal posters (minimum wage, OSHA, FMLA where it applies, EEO, employee polygraph protection, USERRA) and your state's posters where employees can see them, and give remote employees electronic copies. Replace them when the agencies update them.
obligations.penalty: Fines per poster, up to about $25,000 for the OSHA poster; more often, a missing poster extends the time an employee has to bring a claim
obligations.explanation: Federal and state law require a set of notices on the wall, or on the intranet for remote staff. The Department of Labor's poster advisor lists the federal ones for free; the state labor agency lists its own. The paid poster services sell the same thing laminated. Check them once a year and whenever the minimum wage changes.

obligations.name: Registered agent in every state of registration
obligations.action: Keep a registered agent appointed in the home state and in every state where the company is registered, keep the agent's invoice paid, and update the Secretary of State within the state's deadline if the agent or its address changes. Add the agent's renewal date as your own date.
obligations.penalty: A resigned or lapsed agent leaves the company without a registered agent; the state revokes or dissolves it after notice, and lawsuits can be served without the company knowing
obligations.explanation: Every corporation, LLC and nonprofit must have a registered agent with a street address in each state where it is registered, to receive legal papers and state notices. Commercial agents charge $50 to $300 a year and resign when unpaid, and a company without an agent is on the road to administrative dissolution. The renewal date is the agent's, not the state's, so it belongs on the calendar as your own date.

obligations.name: Beneficial ownership report: not required for US formed companies
obligations.action: Nothing to file. Companies formed in a US state are exempt. A company formed under foreign law and registered to do business in a US state still reports.
obligations.explanation: The Corporate Transparency Act originally required most US companies to report their owners to FinCEN, with penalties of $591 a day. An interim rule in March 2025 exempted US formed companies, and a final rule effective August 14, 2026 made that exemption permanent. The federal rule does not change state requirements: New York's LLC Transparency Act, in force since January 1, 2026, has its own disclosure for LLCs.

obligations.name: Alabama business privilege tax return
obligations.action: File the business privilege tax return with the Alabama Department of Revenue and pay the fee (Tax computed on net worth; entities owing $100 or less are exempt from the tax and from filing since 2024).
obligations.fee: Tax computed on net worth; entities owing $100 or less are exempt from the tax and from filing since 2024
obligations.penalty: 10% of the tax for late filing, plus interest
obligations.explanation: Alabama no longer requires a separate annual report with the Secretary of State for domestic entities. What remains is the business privilege tax return filed with the Department of Revenue: Form CPT for C corporations, due with the corporate income tax return. Since the 2024 tax year, an entity whose tax would be $100 or less owes nothing and does not file.

obligations.name: Alabama charitable organization registration renewal
obligations.agency: Alabama Attorney General, Consumer Protection Division
obligations.action: Renew the charitable organization registration with the Attorney General within 90 days after the fiscal year ends, with the financial report or Form 990.
obligations.penalty: Up to $5,000 per violation for soliciting while unregistered
obligations.explanation: A charity that asks Alabama residents for contributions registers with the Attorney General before it starts and renews every year within 90 days after its fiscal year ends, March 31 for a calendar year. The fee is $25. Religious organizations, schools, and charities raising under $25,000 a year with no paid fundraisers are exempt.

obligations.name: Alabama corporate income tax return
obligations.action: File the Alabama corporate income tax return with the Alabama Department of Revenue by the 15th day of the 4th month after the fiscal year ends (April 15 for a calendar year) and pay any tax due. Most states follow the federal extension if one is filed.
obligations.explanation: Alabama taxes corporate income, so a C corporation doing business there files a state return with the Alabama Department of Revenue by the 15th day of the 4th month after the fiscal year ends (April 15 for a calendar year), the same day as the federal Form 1120. The state usually honors a federal extension to file, but not to pay. The form name and any minimum tax are on the state's site.

obligations.name: Alabama corporate estimated tax payment
obligations.form: The state's estimated tax voucher or online payment
obligations.action: Pay the Alabama corporate estimated tax installment if the year's state tax will pass the state's threshold.
obligations.penalty: Underpayment interest, and in some states a penalty, on each short installment
obligations.explanation: Like the IRS, Alabama collects corporate income tax during the year once the expected tax passes a threshold the state sets (a few hundred to a thousand dollars in most states). The installments fall on the 15th day of the fourth, sixth, ninth and twelfth months of the fiscal year in most states, the same days as the federal ones; the Alabama Department of Revenue page has the threshold and any state that differs. Shown for every C corporation because the threshold is low; a corporation expecting no state tax can mark the lines handled.

obligations.name: Alabama pass through entity return
obligations.action: File the Alabama pass through entity return with the Alabama Department of Revenue by the 15th day of the 3rd month after the fiscal year ends (March 15 for a calendar year), with the owners' state K-1s.
obligations.explanation: An S corporation or partnership doing business in Alabama files a state information return by the 15th day of the 3rd month after the fiscal year ends (March 15 for a calendar year), alongside the federal return, so the owners can report their shares on their own Alabama returns. Some states charge a minimum tax or filing fee with it; check the Alabama Department of Revenue page.

obligations.name: Alabama personal income tax return with business income
obligations.action: Report the business income on the owner's Alabama personal return by April 15 each year.
obligations.explanation: A sole proprietorship or single member LLC reports its income on the owner's Alabama personal return, due April 15 each year in step with the federal Form 1040.

obligations.name: Alabama unemployment insurance wage report
obligations.action: File the quarterly wage report and pay state unemployment insurance contributions for employees working in Alabama.
obligations.penalty: Late filing and payment penalties set by the state, plus loss of the federal FUTA credit if contributions are not paid on time
obligations.explanation: An employer registers for unemployment insurance in each state where it has employees and files a wage report every quarter, by the last day of the month after the quarter in nearly every state: April 30, July 31, October 31 and January 31. The contribution rate is set by the state each year. Paying on time also earns the 5.4% credit against the federal unemployment tax.

obligations.name: Alabama annual withholding reconciliation
obligations.action: File the annual reconciliation of Alabama income tax withheld, with copies of the W-2s, and keep withholding deposits on the schedule the state assigned.
obligations.explanation: Alabama withholds state income tax from employee wages, and the employer reconciles the year's withholding with the Alabama Department of Revenue after year end, by January 31 in most states and the end of February in a few, with copies of the W-2s where the state takes them. Withholding deposits during the year follow a schedule the state assigns, monthly or quarterly for most small employers. A payroll provider normally handles both.

obligations.name: Alabama sales tax return
obligations.action: File the Alabama sales tax return and remit the tax collected, on the monthly, quarterly or annual schedule the state assigned.
obligations.penalty: Late filing and payment penalties plus interest; personal liability for the owners for tax collected and not remitted
obligations.explanation: A business that collects Alabama sales tax files returns on a schedule the Alabama Department of Revenue assigns from its volume: monthly for larger sellers, quarterly for most small ones, annually for the smallest. Dates here assume quarterly, due the 20th of the month after the quarter. Sales tax collected belongs to the state, and owners can be held personally liable for it.

obligations.name: Alaska charitable organization registration renewal

obligations.action: Renew the state business license before it expires on December 31.
obligations.fee: $50 a year, or $100 for two years
obligations.explanation: Alaska requires a state business license for every business operating in the state, separate from the entity's registration. It expires December 31 and renews for one or two years.

obligations.name: Arizona annual report

obligations.penalty: $9 a month late; administrative dissolution after 60 days past due
obligations.explanation: Arizona corporations file an annual report with the Arizona Corporation Commission on the anniversary date the Commission assigned at incorporation. Arizona LLCs file no annual report at all, which is one of the reasons the LLC is popular there.

obligations.name: Arizona nonprofit annual report

obligations.name: Arizona charitable solicitation registration: not required
obligations.action: Nothing to file. Arizona repealed general charitable registration in 2013; only veterans organizations soliciting in the state register.

A charity asking Arizona residents for money needs no state registration, though it still files its Form 990 and keeps its corporate standing. obligations.penalty: Revocation after continued failure
obligations.explanation: An Arkansas nonprofit corporation files an annual report with the Secretary of State by August 1, with no fee. It can be filed from January 1.

obligations.fee: No fee
obligations.penalty: Civil penalties and an order to stop soliciting
obligations.explanation: A charity that solicits in Arkansas registers with the Secretary of State and files an annual report within six months after its fiscal year ends, June 30 for a calendar year. obligations.penalty: $250 penalty from the Franchise Tax Board; suspension after continued failure
obligations.explanation: California corporations file a Statement of Information every year, due by the last day of the month in which the corporation was registered. The filing window opens five months before that. The penalty for missing it is $250, assessed by the Franchise Tax Board, and a corporation that stays delinquent is suspended.

obligations.name: California statement of information
obligations.action: File the statement of information with the California Secretary of State and pay the fee ($20).
obligations.penalty: $250 penalty from the Franchise Tax Board; suspension after continued failure
obligations.explanation: California LLCs file a Statement of Information every two years, due by the last day of the anniversary month of registration. The penalty for missing it is $250, assessed by the Franchise Tax Board, and an LLC that stays delinquent is suspended.

The fee is $20. It is separate from the Attorney General's charity registration and from the Franchise Tax Board's exempt organization return (Form 199 or the 199N e-Postcard), which is due at the same time as the federal Form 990.

obligations.name: California charity registration renewal
obligations.agency: California Attorney General, Registry of Charities and Fundraisers
obligations.action: File the annual registration renewal fee report (Form RRF-1) with a copy of the Form 990 (or Form CT-TR-1 if the charity files the 990-N) and the renewal fee, four months and fifteen days after the fiscal year ends; the IRS extension carries over.
obligations.fee: $25 to $1,200, by total revenue
obligations.penalty: Late fees, loss of tax exemption with the Franchise Tax Board, and suspension of the right to solicit
obligations.explanation: Every charity that holds assets or solicits in California is on the Attorney General's Registry and renews every year on Form RRF-1, due four months and fifteen days after the fiscal year ends, May 15 for a calendar year, with the same extension as the Form 990. The fee runs from $25 for revenue under $50,000 to $1,200 above $500 million, in nine tiers. A charity that files the 990-N e-Postcard attaches the Attorney General's own financial form, CT-TR-1, since the e-Postcard carries no figures. A registry that lapses leads to loss of the state tax exemption, so this one is worth a reminder.

obligations.name: California annual LLC tax
obligations.action: Pay the $800 annual LLC tax with Form 3522 by the 15th day of the fourth month of the tax year.
obligations.penalty: 5% of the unpaid tax plus 0.5% a month, plus interest
obligations.explanation: Every LLC registered or doing business in California and taxed as a partnership or a disregarded entity pays an $800 annual tax to the Franchise Tax Board, whether or not it made money. It is due by the 15th day of the fourth month of the tax year, April 15 for a calendar year, which means it is paid in advance for the current year. An LLC that elected corporate treatment files Form 100 or 100S and pays the corporate minimum franchise tax instead.

obligations.name: California LLC fee estimate (California income over $250,000)
obligations.action: Pay the estimated LLC fee with Form 3536 if California income will exceed $250,000.
obligations.fee: $900 to $11,790 depending on California income over $250,000
obligations.penalty: 10% of the underpaid fee
obligations.explanation: On top of the $800 tax, an LLC taxed as a partnership or disregarded entity with California income over $250,000 pays a fee that scales with income. The estimate is due by the 15th day of the sixth month, June 15 for a calendar year, and the rest with the return. The line is shown from the $100,000 to $500,000 revenue band because the fee starts at $250,000; an LLC below that owes nothing.

obligations.name: California LLC return
obligations.action: File Form 568 for the LLC with the Franchise Tax Board by the 15th day of the third month after the year ends, with a Schedule K-1 (568) for each member.
obligations.explanation: A California LLC taxed as a partnership files Form 568 with the Franchise Tax Board by the 15th day of the third month after the year ends, March 15 for a calendar year, with an automatic extension to file (not to pay). The $800 annual tax and any LLC fee are reconciled on it.

obligations.name: California single member LLC return
obligations.action: File Form 568 for the single member LLC with the Franchise Tax Board by the 15th day of the fourth month after the year ends, the same day as the owner's return.
obligations.explanation: A single member LLC is disregarded for income tax but still files its own Form 568 with the Franchise Tax Board, by the 15th day of the fourth month after the year ends, April 15 for a calendar year, with an automatic extension to file. The $800 annual tax and any LLC fee are reconciled on it.

obligations.name: California S corporation estimated tax and minimum franchise tax
obligations.action: Pay the S corporation's estimated tax in four installments on the 15th day of the fourth, sixth, ninth and twelfth months of the tax year; the $800 minimum goes with the first.
obligations.fee: $800 minimum franchise tax, paid with the first installment; 1.5% of California net income
obligations.penalty: Underpayment penalty plus interest; 5% plus 0.5% a month on late payments
obligations.explanation: California taxes S corporations at 1.5% of net income with an $800 minimum franchise tax, owed in loss years too, and collects it through estimated payments on the 15th day of the fourth, sixth, ninth and twelfth months of the tax year: April 15, June 15, September 15 and December 15 for a calendar year. The $800 minimum is paid with the first installment. The S corporation's first tax year is exempt from the minimum. An LLC that elected S corporation treatment pays this instead of the LLC tax.

obligations.name: California exempt organization annual return
obligations.action: File Form 199, or the 199N e-Postcard if gross receipts are normally $50,000 or less (private foundations file Form 199 at any size), with the Franchise Tax Board by the 15th day of the fifth month after the fiscal year ends, the same day as the federal return.
obligations.fee: No fee
obligations.penalty: $5 a month late, up to $40; revocation of the state exemption after continued failure
obligations.explanation: California runs its own exemption alongside the federal one, and an exempt organization files a state return with the Franchise Tax Board every year: Form 199, or the 199N e-Postcard for gross receipts normally $50,000 or less. A private foundation files Form 199 whatever its size. It is due by the 15th day of the fifth month after the fiscal year ends, May 15 for a calendar year, with an automatic extension to the federal extended date. There is no fee since 2021. An organization that stops filing loses its California exemption and is billed the $800 minimum franchise tax.

obligations.name: California corporate income tax return
obligations.action: File the California corporate income tax return with the California Franchise Tax Board by the 15th day of the 4th month after the fiscal year ends (April 15 for a calendar year) and pay any tax due. Most states follow the federal extension if one is filed.
obligations.explanation: California taxes corporate income, so a C corporation doing business there files a state return with the California Franchise Tax Board by the 15th day of the 4th month after the fiscal year ends (April 15 for a calendar year), the same day as the federal Form 1120. The state usually honors a federal extension to file, but not to pay. The form name and any minimum tax are on the state's site.

obligations.name: California corporate estimated tax payment
obligations.action: Pay the California corporate estimated tax installment if the year's state tax will pass the state's threshold.
obligations.fee: $800 minimum franchise tax, paid with the first installment; 8.84% of California net income
obligations.penalty: Underpayment interest, and in some states a penalty, on each short installment
obligations.explanation: Like the IRS, California collects corporate income tax during the year once the expected tax passes a threshold the state sets (a few hundred to a thousand dollars in most states). The installments fall on the 15th day of the fourth, sixth, ninth and twelfth months of the fiscal year in most states, the same days as the federal ones; California's minimum franchise tax of $800 is owed by every corporation registered or doing business in the state, loss years included, and is paid with the first installment; a corporation's first tax year is exempt from the minimum. Shown for every C corporation because the threshold is low; a corporation expecting no state tax can mark the lines handled.

obligations.name: California pass through entity return
obligations.action: File the California pass through entity return with the California Franchise Tax Board by the 15th day of the 3rd month after the fiscal year ends (March 15 for a calendar year), with the owners' state K-1s.
obligations.explanation: An S corporation or partnership doing business in California files a state information return by the 15th day of the 3rd month after the fiscal year ends (March 15 for a calendar year), alongside the federal return, so the owners can report their shares on their own California returns. Some states charge a minimum tax or filing fee with it; check the California Franchise Tax Board page.

obligations.name: California personal income tax return with business income
obligations.action: Report the business income on the owner's California personal return by April 15 each year.
obligations.explanation: A sole proprietorship or single member LLC reports its income on the owner's California personal return, due April 15 each year in step with the federal Form 1040.

obligations.name: California unemployment insurance wage report
obligations.action: File the quarterly wage report and pay state unemployment insurance contributions for employees working in California.
obligations.penalty: Late filing and payment penalties set by the state, plus loss of the federal FUTA credit if contributions are not paid on time
obligations.explanation: An employer registers for unemployment insurance in each state where it has employees and files a wage report every quarter, by the last day of the month after the quarter in nearly every state: April 30, July 31, October 31 and January 31. The contribution rate is set by the state each year. Paying on time also earns the 5.4% credit against the federal unemployment tax.

obligations.name: California fourth quarter wage reports closing the year
obligations.action: File the fourth quarter DE 9 and DE 9C with the Employment Development Department by January 31 and keep withholding deposits on the schedule the EDD assigned. California has no separate annual reconciliation and W-2s are not filed with the state.
obligations.explanation: California reconciles withholding every quarter rather than once a year: the DE 9 (contributions and withholding) and DE 9C (wage detail) are due by the last day of the month after each quarter, and the fourth quarter filing, due January 31, closes the year. W-2 copies go to the Social Security Administration only. A payroll provider files both forms.

obligations.name: California disability insurance and paid family leave withholding
obligations.action: Withhold and remit the contributions through payroll, or keep the policy in force, as the program requires; there is no separate return.
obligations.explanation: California's state disability insurance and paid family leave are funded by a deduction from employee wages at a rate the EDD sets each year, withheld and remitted with regular payroll and reported on the quarterly DE 9 and DE 9C. There is no separate filing.

obligations.name: California harassment prevention training (5 or more employees)
obligations.agency: California labor and civil rights agencies
obligations.action: Schedule this year's sexual harassment prevention training for employees working in California and keep the attendance records.
obligations.explanation: California requires private employers to train employees on preventing sexual harassment. Every two years: two hours for supervisors and one hour for other employees, for employers with five or more employees. The date here is a planning reminder at the start of the year; the legal timing runs from each employee's hire date and the last training.

obligations.name: California retirement savings mandate (CalSavers)
obligations.form: Registration with the state program, then payroll deductions
obligations.action: Register with CalSavers if the company has any employees in California and no retirement plan of its own, then run the employee deductions through payroll; or certify that the company has its own plan.
obligations.penalty: Per employee penalties after notice, set by the state
obligations.explanation: California requires an employer with no retirement plan of its own to enroll its employees in the state program, CalSavers, which runs Roth IRAs funded by payroll deductions. The employer registers, uploads its employees and passes the deductions through; it contributes nothing and the employees can opt out. An employer that sponsors a 401(k), SIMPLE IRA or other plan certifies its exemption instead. From 2025 every employer with at least one employee and no plan registers; penalties start at $250 per eligible employee after notice and rise to $500. Registration deadlines have passed for existing employers, so a company not yet registered should register now; a new employer registers within the program's window after its first hire.

obligations.name: California sales tax return
obligations.action: File the California sales tax return and remit the tax collected, on the monthly, quarterly or annual schedule the state assigned.
obligations.penalty: Late filing and payment penalties plus interest; personal liability for the owners for tax collected and not remitted
obligations.explanation: A business that collects California sales tax files returns on a schedule the California Franchise Tax Board assigns from its volume: monthly for larger sellers, quarterly for most small ones, annually for the smallest. Dates here assume quarterly, due the last day of the month after the quarter. Sales tax collected belongs to the state, and owners can be held personally liable for it.

obligations.name: Colorado periodic report
obligations.action: File the periodic report with the Colorado Secretary of State and pay the fee ($25).
obligations.penalty: $50 late fee; delinquent status after the two month grace period
obligations.explanation: Colorado calls its annual report a periodic report. It is due by the last day of the anniversary month of formation, can be filed up to two months early, and costs $25 online since July 2024. Two months after the due date the entity becomes delinquent and the fee rises.

obligations.name: Colorado periodic report
obligations.action: File the periodic report with the Colorado Secretary of State and pay the fee ($25).
obligations.penalty: $50 late fee; delinquent status after the two month grace period
obligations.explanation: Colorado requires every LLC registered in the state to file a periodic report with the Colorado Secretary of State by the last day of the anniversary month of its formation. The fee is $25. Miss it and the result is $50 late fee; delinquent status after the two month grace period. A company registered in more than one state files this in each of them.

obligations.name: Colorado periodic report
obligations.action: File the periodic report with the Colorado Secretary of State and pay the fee ($25).
obligations.penalty: $50 late fee; delinquent status after the two month grace period
obligations.explanation: Colorado requires every limited partnership or LLP registered in the state to file a periodic report with the Colorado Secretary of State by the last day of the anniversary month of its formation. The fee is $25. Miss it and the result is $50 late fee; delinquent status after the two month grace period. A company registered in more than one state files this in each of them. A general partnership that never registered with the state files no annual report in most states; the line is for limited partnerships and LLPs.

obligations.name: Colorado nonprofit periodic report
obligations.action: File the periodic report with the Colorado Secretary of State and pay the fee ($25).
obligations.penalty: $50 late fee; delinquent status after the two month grace period
obligations.explanation: Colorado requires every nonprofit corporation registered in the state to file a periodic report with the Colorado Secretary of State by the last day of the anniversary month of its formation. obligations.name: Colorado charitable organization registration renewal
obligations.agency: Colorado Secretary of State, Charities Program
obligations.action: Renew the charitable organization registration online with the Secretary of State, with the financial information from the Form 990, four and a half months after the fiscal year ends.
obligations.penalty: Expiration of the registration and a fine for soliciting while expired
obligations.explanation: A charity that solicits in Colorado registers with the Secretary of State before it starts and renews every year four and a half months after its fiscal year ends, May 15 for a calendar year, with an extension that follows the IRS extension. The fee is $10.

obligations.name: Colorado corporate income tax return
obligations.action: File the Colorado corporate income tax return with the Colorado Department of Revenue by the 15th day of the 4th month after the fiscal year ends (April 15 for a calendar year) and pay any tax due. Most states follow the federal extension if one is filed.
obligations.explanation: Colorado taxes corporate income, so a C corporation doing business there files a state return with the Colorado Department of Revenue by the 15th day of the 4th month after the fiscal year ends (April 15 for a calendar year), the same day as the federal Form 1120. The state usually honors a federal extension to file, but not to pay. The form name and any minimum tax are on the state's site.

obligations.name: Colorado corporate estimated tax payment

obligations.action: Pay the Colorado corporate estimated tax installment if the year's state tax will pass the state's threshold.
obligations.penalty: Underpayment interest, and in some states a penalty, on each short installment
obligations.explanation: Like the IRS, Colorado collects corporate income tax during the year once the expected tax passes a threshold the state sets (a few hundred to a thousand dollars in most states). obligations.explanation: Colorado withholds state income tax from employee wages, and the employer reconciles the year's withholding with the Colorado Department of Revenue after year end, by January 31 in most states and the end of February in a few, with copies of the W-2s where the state takes them. Withholding deposits during the year follow a schedule the state assigns, monthly or quarterly for most small employers. A payroll provider normally handles both.

obligations.name: Colorado FAMLI premium report
obligations.action: File the quarterly premium report and pay the contributions by the last day of the month after the quarter: April 30, July 31, October 31 and January 31.
obligations.penalty: Interest and late penalties set by the program on premiums paid late
obligations.explanation: Colorado's paid family and medical leave program is funded by a premium on wages set each year, split evenly between employer and employee (employers with fewer than ten employees pay no employer share), reported every quarter to the FAMLI Division with a wage report of its own. The rate is set by the program each year, so the figure on the agency page is the one to use, and a payroll provider normally files the report.

obligations.name: Colorado retirement savings mandate (Colorado SecureSavings, 5 or more employees)
obligations.form: Registration with the state program, then payroll deductions
obligations.action: Register with Colorado SecureSavings if the company has 5 or more employees in Colorado and no retirement plan of its own, then run the employee deductions through payroll; or certify that the company has its own plan.

obligations.name: Connecticut annual report
obligations.action: File the annual report with the Connecticut Secretary of the State and pay the fee ($150).
obligations.penalty: Administrative dissolution after continued failure
obligations.explanation: Connecticut requires every corporation registered in the state to file an annual report with the Connecticut Secretary of the State by the last day of the anniversary month of its formation. The fee is $150. Miss it and the result is administrative dissolution after continued failure. A company registered in more than one state files this in each of them.

obligations.name: Connecticut annual report
obligations.action: File the annual report with the Connecticut Secretary of the State and pay the fee ($80).
obligations.penalty: Administrative dissolution after continued failure
obligations.explanation: Connecticut LLCs file their annual report between January 1 and March 31 each year, a change made in 2020 from the old anniversary month rule. The fee is $80.

obligations.name: Connecticut annual report
obligations.action: File the annual report with the Connecticut Secretary of the State and pay the fee ($80).
obligations.penalty: Administrative dissolution after continued failure
obligations.explanation: Connecticut LLCs file their annual report between January 1 and March 31 each year, a change made in 2020 from the old anniversary month rule. The fee is $80. A general partnership that never registered with the state files no annual report in most states.

obligations.name: Connecticut nonprofit annual report
obligations.action: File the annual report with the Connecticut Secretary of the State and pay the fee ($50).
obligations.penalty: Administrative dissolution after continued failure
obligations.explanation: Connecticut requires every nonprofit corporation registered in the state to file an annual report with the Connecticut Secretary of the State on the anniversary date of its formation. The fee is $50. Miss it and the result is administrative dissolution after continued failure. A nonprofit registered in more than one state files this in each of them.

obligations.name: Connecticut charitable organization registration renewal
obligations.agency: Connecticut Department of Consumer Protection, Public Charities Unit
obligations.action: Renew the charitable organization registration with the Department of Consumer Protection by the last day of the eleventh month after the fiscal year ends, with the Form 990.
obligations.penalty: $25 a month late
obligations.explanation: A charity that solicits in Connecticut registers with the Department of Consumer Protection and renews every year by the last day of the eleventh month after its fiscal year ends, November 30 for a calendar year. The fee is $50 and the late fee accrues monthly. Charities raising under $50,000 a year with no paid staff, religious organizations and schools are exempt.

obligations.name: Connecticut corporate income tax return
obligations.action: File the Connecticut corporate income tax return with the Connecticut Department of Revenue Services by the 1st day of the 5th month after the fiscal year ends (May 1 for a calendar year) and pay any tax due. Most states follow the federal extension if one is filed.
obligations.explanation: Connecticut taxes corporate income, so a C corporation doing business there files a state return with the Connecticut Department of Revenue Services by the 1st day of the 5th month after the fiscal year ends (May 1 for a calendar year), later than the federal Form 1120. The state usually honors a federal extension to file, but not to pay. The form name and any minimum tax are on the state's site.

obligations.name: Connecticut Paid Leave contributions
obligations.action: File the quarterly premium report and pay the contributions by the last day of the month after the quarter: April 30, July 31, October 31 and January 31.
obligations.penalty: Interest and late penalties set by the program on premiums paid late
obligations.explanation: Connecticut Paid Leave is funded by an employee deduction of 0.5% of wages, no employer share, which the employer withholds and remits every quarter through the Paid Leave Authority's portal. The rate is set by the program each year, so the figure on the agency page is the one to use, and a payroll provider normally files the report.

obligations.name: Connecticut harassment prevention training (3 or more employees)
obligations.agency: Connecticut labor and civil rights agencies
obligations.action: Schedule this year's sexual harassment prevention training for employees working in Connecticut and keep the attendance records.
obligations.explanation: Connecticut requires private employers to train employees on preventing sexual harassment. Two hours for all employees within six months of hire, for employers with three or more employees (supervisors only below three), with a refresher every ten years. The date here is a planning reminder at the start of the year; the legal timing runs from each employee's hire date and the last training.

obligations.form: Registration with the state program, then payroll deductions
obligations.action: Register with MyCTSavings if the company has 5 or more employees in Connecticut and no retirement plan of its own, then run the employee deductions through payroll; or certify that the company has its own plan.

The employer registers, uploads its employees and passes the deductions through; it contributes nothing and the employees can opt out. An employer that sponsors a 401(k), SIMPLE IRA or other plan certifies its exemption instead.
