obligations.name: Delaware annual report and franchise tax
obligations.action: File the annual report and franchise tax with the Delaware Division of Corporations and pay the fee: $50 report fee plus franchise tax, $175 minimum (authorized shares method) or $400 minimum (assumed par value capital method).
obligations.fee: $50 report fee plus franchise tax, $175 minimum (authorized shares method) or $400 minimum (assumed par value capital method)
obligations.penalty: $200 late penalty plus 1.5% interest a month on the unpaid tax
obligations.explanation: Every Delaware corporation files an annual report and pays franchise tax by March 1, online with the Division of Corporations. The tax is computed by one of two methods, and a startup with a large authorized share count should always check the assumed par value method, which usually brings the bill down to $400. Missing March 1 costs $200 plus interest, and a corporation that stays unpaid for a year has its charter voided.

obligations.name: Delaware foreign corporation annual report
obligations.action: File the foreign corporation annual report with the Delaware Division of Corporations and pay the fee ($250).
obligations.penalty: $250 penalty for a report not filed, plus loss of good standing
obligations.explanation: A corporation formed in another state and qualified to do business in Delaware files a foreign corporation annual report with the Division of Corporations by June 30 and pays $250. It owes no Delaware franchise tax; that is for corporations formed in Delaware. The fee rose from $125 to $250 on August 1, 2026.

obligations.name: Delaware annual LLC tax
obligations.action: File the annual LLC tax with the Delaware Division of Corporations and pay the fee ($400).
obligations.penalty: $200 late penalty plus 1.5% interest a month
obligations.explanation: Delaware LLCs file no annual report. They pay a flat $400 annual tax by June 1, online with the Division of Corporations; it was $300 until House Bill 400 raised it in 2026, so the payment due June 1, 2027 is the first at the new amount. A late payment costs $200 plus interest, and an LLC that stays unpaid loses its certificate of formation.

obligations.name: Delaware annual partnership tax
obligations.action: File the annual partnership tax with the Delaware Division of Corporations and pay the fee: $400 for a limited partnership ($300 per partner for an LLP, up to $180,000).
obligations.fee: $400 for a limited partnership ($300 per partner for an LLP, up to $180,000)
obligations.penalty: $200 late penalty plus 1.5% interest a month
obligations.explanation: A Delaware limited partnership files no annual report. It pays a flat $400 annual tax by June 1, online with the Division of Corporations, raised from $300 by House Bill 400 in 2026. A limited liability partnership pays $300 per partner instead, up to $180,000. A late payment costs $200 plus interest. A general partnership that never registered with the state files no annual report in most states.

obligations.name: Delaware nonprofit annual report
obligations.action: File the annual report with the Delaware Division of Corporations and pay the fee ($25).
obligations.penalty: $200 late penalty plus interest
obligations.explanation: A Delaware nonstock corporation that is exempt from franchise tax files an annual report by March 1 and pays a $25 fee, with no franchise tax. The exemption is claimed on the report itself with a copy of the IRS determination letter.

obligations.name: Delaware charitable solicitation registration: not required
obligations.action: Nothing to file. Delaware has no charitable solicitation registration.
obligations.explanation: Delaware is one of the states that never required charities to register before soliciting. A Delaware charity still files its Form 990 and its annual report with the Division of Corporations, and registers in any other state where it asks for money.

obligations.name: Delaware business license renewal
obligations.action: Renew the Delaware business license with the Division of Revenue before it expires on December 31; licenses can be renewed for one or three years.
obligations.fee: $75 a year for the first location, $25 for each additional
obligations.penalty: Operating without a license is a violation; the Division assesses the license fee plus penalties and interest
obligations.explanation: A company that actually operates in Delaware, with an office, staff or sales there, holds a state business license from the Division of Revenue, separate from its registration with the Division of Corporations. A Delaware company based in another state does not need one. The license expires December 31 and renews online for $75 a year.

obligations.name: Delaware gross receipts tax return
obligations.action: File the gross receipts tax return and pay the tax on Delaware receipts above the exclusion, monthly by the 20th or quarterly by the last day of the month after the quarter as the Division assigned.
obligations.fee: 0.0945% to 0.7468% of gross receipts by activity, after an exclusion of $100,000 a month ($300,000 a quarter) for most businesses
obligations.penalty: 5% a month late, up to 50%, plus interest
obligations.explanation: Delaware has no sales tax; businesses operating in the state pay a tax on their own gross receipts instead, at a rate set by the kind of business. Most small businesses fall under the $100,000 a month exclusion and file quarterly returns showing no tax, which are still due. A Delaware company based elsewhere owes nothing here. Dates assume quarterly filing.

obligations.name: Delaware franchise tax installment (if last year's tax was $5,000 or more)
obligations.action: Pay the quarterly franchise tax installment if last year's franchise tax was $5,000 or more.
obligations.fee: 40%, 20% and 20% of the prior year's tax, with the balance on March 1
obligations.explanation: A Delaware corporation whose franchise tax was $5,000 or more pays it in installments: 40% by June 1, 20% by September 1, 20% by December 1, and the rest with the annual report on March 1. Smaller corporations pay once, on March 1. The test is the tax, not revenue; the line is shown from the $1 million revenue band because a corporation below it rarely owes $5,000 under the assumed par value method, and a corporation that does can add the dates as its own.

obligations.name: Delaware corporate income tax return
obligations.action: File the Delaware corporate income tax return with the Delaware Division of Revenue by the 15th day of the 4th month after the fiscal year ends (April 15 for a calendar year) and pay any tax due. Most states follow the federal extension if one is filed.
obligations.explanation: Delaware taxes corporate income, so a C corporation doing business there files a state return with the Delaware Division of Revenue by the 15th day of the 4th month after the fiscal year ends (April 15 for a calendar year), the same day as the federal Form 1120. The state usually honors a federal extension to file, but not to pay. The form name and any minimum tax are on the state's site. A corporation formed in Delaware but based elsewhere, with no Delaware operations, files the annual report and franchise tax instead and owes no Form 1100.

obligations.name: Delaware corporate estimated tax payment
obligations.form: The state's estimated tax voucher or online payment
obligations.action: Pay the Delaware corporate estimated tax installment if the year's state tax will pass the state's threshold.
obligations.penalty: Underpayment interest, and in some states a penalty, on each short installment
obligations.explanation: Like the IRS, Delaware collects corporate income tax during the year once the expected tax passes a threshold the state sets (a few hundred to a thousand dollars in most states). The installments fall on the 15th day of the fourth, sixth, ninth and twelfth months of the fiscal year in most states, the same days as the federal ones; the Delaware Division of Revenue page has the threshold and any state that differs. Shown for every C corporation because the threshold is low; a corporation expecting no state tax can mark the lines handled.

obligations.name: Delaware pass through entity return
obligations.action: File the Delaware pass through entity return with the Delaware Division of Revenue by the 15th day of the 3rd month after the fiscal year ends (March 15 for a calendar year), with the owners' state K-1s.
obligations.explanation: An S corporation or partnership doing business in Delaware files a state information return by the 15th day of the 3rd month after the fiscal year ends (March 15 for a calendar year), alongside the federal return, so the owners can report their shares on their own Delaware returns. Some states charge a minimum tax or filing fee with it; check the Delaware Division of Revenue page.

obligations.name: Delaware personal income tax return with business income
obligations.action: Report the business income on the owner's Delaware personal return by April 30 each year.
obligations.explanation: A sole proprietorship or single member LLC reports its income on the owner's Delaware personal return, due April 30 each year, later than the federal Form 1040.

obligations.name: Delaware unemployment insurance wage report
obligations.action: File the quarterly wage report and pay state unemployment insurance contributions for employees working in Delaware.
obligations.penalty: Late filing and payment penalties set by the state, plus loss of the federal FUTA credit if contributions are not paid on time
obligations.explanation: An employer registers for unemployment insurance in each state where it has employees and files a wage report every quarter, by the last day of the month after the quarter in nearly every state: April 30, July 31, October 31 and January 31. The contribution rate is set by the state each year. Paying on time also earns the 5.4% credit against the federal unemployment tax.

obligations.name: Delaware annual withholding reconciliation
obligations.action: File the annual reconciliation of Delaware income tax withheld, with copies of the W-2s, and keep withholding deposits on the schedule the state assigned.
obligations.explanation: Delaware withholds state income tax from employee wages, and the employer reconciles the year's withholding with the Delaware Division of Revenue after year end, by January 31 in most states and the end of February in a few, with copies of the W-2s where the state takes them. Withholding deposits during the year follow a schedule the state assigns, monthly or quarterly for most small employers. A payroll provider normally handles both.

obligations.name: Delaware Paid Leave contributions
obligations.action: File the quarterly premium report and pay the contributions by the last day of the month after the quarter: April 30, July 31, October 31 and January 31.
obligations.penalty: Interest and late penalties set by the program on premiums paid late
obligations.explanation: Delaware's paid family and medical leave program collects contributions from January 2025 at a rate set each year, with up to half deducted from wages, reported every quarter through the Department of Labor's LaborFirst portal. Employers with fewer than ten employees are exempt from most of it and those with 10 to 24 owe only the parental leave part. The rate is set by the program each year, so the figure on the agency page is the one to use, and a payroll provider normally files the report.

obligations.name: Delaware harassment prevention training (50 or more employees)
obligations.agency: Delaware labor and civil rights agencies
obligations.action: Schedule this year's sexual harassment prevention training for employees working in Delaware and keep the attendance records.
obligations.explanation: Delaware requires private employers to train employees on preventing sexual harassment. Every two years, for employers with 50 or more employees. The date here is a planning reminder at the start of the year; the legal timing runs from each employee's hire date and the last training.

obligations.name: Delaware retirement savings mandate (Delaware EARNS, 5 or more employees)
obligations.form: Registration with the state program, then payroll deductions
obligations.action: Register with Delaware EARNS if the company has 5 or more employees in Delaware and no retirement plan of its own, then run the employee deductions through payroll; or certify that the company has its own plan.
obligations.penalty: Per employee penalties after notice, set by the state
obligations.explanation: Delaware requires an employer with no retirement plan of its own to enroll its employees in the state program, Delaware EARNS, which runs Roth IRAs funded by payroll deductions. The employer registers, uploads its employees and passes the deductions through; it contributes nothing and the employees can opt out. An employer that sponsors a 401(k), SIMPLE IRA or other plan certifies its exemption instead. Registration deadlines have passed for existing employers, so a company not yet registered should register now; a new employer registers within the program's window after its first hire.

obligations.name: Delaware sales tax: no state sales tax
obligations.action: Nothing to file with the state. Delaware has no sales tax. Businesses operating in the state pay the gross receipts tax on their own receipts instead, which is on this calendar for a company with people in Delaware.
obligations.explanation: Delaware has no sales tax. Businesses operating in the state pay the gross receipts tax on their own receipts instead, which is on this calendar for a company with people in Delaware. A company that ticked Delaware as a state where it collects sales tax has no state return to file there.

obligations.name: District of Columbia biennial report
obligations.agency: DC Department of Licensing and Consumer Protection
obligations.action: File the biennial report with the DC Department of Licensing and Consumer Protection and pay the fee ($300).
obligations.penalty: $100 late fee; revocation after continued failure
obligations.explanation: DC entities file a two year report (Form BRA-25) with the Corporations Division by April 1 of the year after registration and every second year after that. The fee is $300 and the late fee $100. A company formed elsewhere counts from the year it registered in DC.

obligations.name: District of Columbia biennial report
obligations.agency: DC Department of Licensing and Consumer Protection
obligations.action: File the biennial report with the DC Department of Licensing and Consumer Protection and pay the fee ($300).
obligations.penalty: $100 late fee; revocation after continued failure
obligations.explanation: District of Columbia requires every LLC registered in the state to file a biennial report with the DC Department of Licensing and Consumer Protection by April 1 of the year after formation and every second year after that. The fee is $300. Miss it and the result is $100 late fee; revocation after continued failure. A company registered in more than one state files this in each of them.

obligations.name: District of Columbia biennial report
obligations.agency: DC Department of Licensing and Consumer Protection
obligations.action: File the biennial report with the DC Department of Licensing and Consumer Protection and pay the fee ($300).
obligations.penalty: $100 late fee; revocation after continued failure
obligations.explanation: District of Columbia requires every limited partnership or LLP registered in the state to file a biennial report with the DC Department of Licensing and Consumer Protection by April 1 of the year after formation and every second year after that. The fee is $300. Miss it and the result is $100 late fee; revocation after continued failure. A company registered in more than one state files this in each of them. A general partnership that never registered with the state files no annual report in most states; the line is for limited partnerships and LLPs.

obligations.name: District of Columbia nonprofit biennial report
obligations.agency: DC Department of Licensing and Consumer Protection
obligations.action: File the biennial report with the DC Department of Licensing and Consumer Protection and pay the fee ($80).
obligations.penalty: $50 late fee; revocation after continued failure
obligations.explanation: A DC nonprofit corporation files a two year report (Form BRA-25) by April 1 of the year after registration and every second year after that. The fee is $80.

obligations.name: DC charitable solicitation license renewal
obligations.agency: DC Department of Licensing and Consumer Protection
obligations.action: Renew the charitable solicitation basic business license with the Department of Licensing and Consumer Protection by the end of the month before the registration month, every two years. There is no extension.
obligations.fee: $99 for two years
obligations.penalty: Fines for soliciting without a license
obligations.explanation: A charity that solicits in the District holds a charitable solicitation license, issued as a basic business license for two or four years, and renews it by the end of the month before its registration month. The fee is $99 for two years. Charities raising under $25,000 a year run entirely by volunteers are exempt. The license needs a DC registered agent and, for a corporation formed elsewhere, foreign registration with the Corporations Division.

obligations.name: DC corporation franchise tax return
obligations.agency: DC Office of Tax and Revenue
obligations.action: File Form D-20 and pay the franchise tax, including the minimum tax even in a loss year.
obligations.fee: Tax on DC net income, $250 minimum ($1,000 if DC gross receipts exceed $1 million)
obligations.penalty: 5% a month late, up to 25%, plus interest
obligations.explanation: A corporation doing business in DC pays the DC corporation franchise tax on Form D-20, due by the 15th day of the fourth month after the year ends. The minimum tax is $250, or $1,000 once DC gross receipts pass $1 million, and it is owed even when the company lost money.

obligations.name: DC unincorporated business franchise tax return
obligations.agency: DC Office of Tax and Revenue
obligations.action: File Form D-30 if the business had DC gross receipts over $12,000.
obligations.fee: Tax on DC net income, $250 minimum ($1,000 if DC gross receipts exceed $1 million)
obligations.penalty: 5% a month late, up to 25%, plus interest
obligations.explanation: DC taxes unincorporated businesses, including LLCs and partnerships, through the unincorporated business franchise tax on Form D-30, due by the 15th day of the fourth month after the year ends, once DC gross receipts exceed $12,000. Businesses whose income comes mainly from the owners' personal services are exempt, which covers many consultants.

obligations.name: DC basic business license renewal
obligations.agency: DC Department of Licensing and Consumer Protection
obligations.action: Keep the basic business license current: it runs two or four years and renews by the end of the month before the month it was issued. Add the renewal date as your own date.
obligations.fee: By endorsement; the general business license is about $200 for two years, plus a $70 application fee and the endorsement fee
obligations.penalty: Fines for operating without a license, and the Department can close the business
obligations.explanation: Every business operating in the District holds a basic business license from the Department of Licensing and Consumer Protection, with an endorsement for its kind of activity (general business for most offices and services). The license runs two or four years from the month it was issued and renews by the end of the month before that month, so the date is the company's own; add it as your own date and the reminders follow. A corporation or LLC formed elsewhere registers with the Corporations Division first. A charity that solicits in DC holds the charitable solicitation endorsement on the same license.

obligations.name: DC personal property tax return
obligations.agency: DC Office of Tax and Revenue
obligations.action: File Form FP-31 reporting the furniture, computers and equipment the business uses in DC as of July 1, by July 31.
obligations.fee: $3.40 per $100 of value above the $225,000 exemption; most small businesses owe nothing but still file
obligations.penalty: 5% a month late, up to 25%, plus interest
obligations.explanation: A business with tangible personal property in the District, computers, furniture and equipment, files a personal property tax return by July 31 each year reporting what it held on July 1. The first $225,000 of value is exempt, so most small businesses pay nothing, but the return is still due.

obligations.name: District of Columbia corporate estimated tax payment
obligations.agency: DC Office of Tax and Revenue
obligations.action: Pay the District of Columbia corporate estimated tax installment if the year's state tax will pass the state's threshold.
obligations.penalty: Underpayment interest, and in some states a penalty, on each short installment
obligations.explanation: Like the IRS, District of Columbia collects corporate income tax during the year once the expected tax passes a threshold the state sets (a few hundred to a thousand dollars in most states). The installments fall on the 15th day of the fourth, sixth, ninth and twelfth months of the fiscal year in most states, the same days as the federal ones; DC calls it the franchise tax; the estimates go to the Office of Tax and Revenue on Form D-20ES once the year's tax is expected to pass $1,000. Shown for every C corporation because the threshold is low; a corporation expecting no state tax can mark the lines handled.

obligations.name: District of Columbia personal income tax return with business income
obligations.agency: DC Office of Tax and Revenue
obligations.action: Report the business income on the owner's District of Columbia personal return by April 15 each year.
obligations.explanation: A sole proprietorship or single member LLC reports its income on the owner's District of Columbia personal return, due April 15 each year in step with the federal Form 1040.

obligations.penalty: Late filing and payment penalties set by the state, plus loss of the federal FUTA credit if contributions are not paid on time
obligations.explanation: An employer registers for unemployment insurance in each state where it has employees and files a wage report every quarter, by the last day of the month after the quarter in nearly every state: April 30, July 31, October 31 and January 31. The contribution rate is set by the state each year. Paying on time also earns the 5.4% credit against the federal unemployment tax.

obligations.name: District of Columbia annual withholding reconciliation
obligations.agency: DC Office of Tax and Revenue
obligations.action: File the annual reconciliation of District of Columbia income tax withheld, with copies of the W-2s, and keep withholding deposits on the schedule the state assigned.
obligations.explanation: District of Columbia withholds state income tax from employee wages, and the employer reconciles the year's withholding with the DC Office of Tax and Revenue after year end, by January 31 in most states and the end of February in a few, with copies of the W-2s where the state takes them. Withholding deposits during the year follow a schedule the state assigns, monthly or quarterly for most small employers. A payroll provider normally handles both.

obligations.name: DC Paid Family Leave contributions
obligations.action: File the quarterly premium report and pay the contributions by the last day of the month after the quarter: April 30, July 31, October 31 and January 31.
obligations.penalty: Interest and late penalties set by the program on premiums paid late
obligations.explanation: The District's paid family leave is funded by an employer paid contribution on wages at a rate set each year, with nothing deducted from employees, reported and paid every quarter with the unemployment insurance wage report. The rate is set by the program each year, so the figure on the agency page is the one to use, and a payroll provider normally files the report.

obligations.name: District of Columbia sales tax return
obligations.agency: DC Office of Tax and Revenue
obligations.action: File the District of Columbia sales tax return and remit the tax collected, on the monthly, quarterly or annual schedule the state assigned.
obligations.penalty: Late filing and payment penalties plus interest; personal liability for the owners for tax collected and not remitted
obligations.explanation: A business that collects District of Columbia sales tax files returns on a schedule the DC Office of Tax and Revenue assigns from its volume: monthly for larger sellers, quarterly for most small ones, annually for the smallest. Dates here assume quarterly, due the 20th of the month after the quarter. Sales tax collected belongs to the state, and owners can be held personally liable for it.

obligations.name: Florida annual report
obligations.action: File the annual report with the Florida Division of Corporations (Sunbiz) and pay the fee ($150).
obligations.penalty: $400 late fee after May 1; administrative dissolution in September
obligations.explanation: Florida annual reports are filed on Sunbiz between January 1 and May 1. The fee is $150 for a corporation and the late fee is a flat $400 the day after May 1, which is one of the steepest in the country. File by the third Friday in September to avoid dissolution; entities still missing are dissolved at the close of business on the fourth Friday of September.

obligations.name: Florida annual report
obligations.action: File the annual report with the Florida Division of Corporations (Sunbiz) and pay the fee ($138.75).
obligations.penalty: $400 late fee after May 1; administrative dissolution in September
obligations.explanation: Florida annual reports are filed on Sunbiz between January 1 and May 1. The fee is $138.75 for an LLC and the late fee is a flat $400 the day after May 1. File by the third Friday in September to avoid dissolution; entities still missing are dissolved at the close of business on the fourth Friday of September.

obligations.name: Florida annual report
obligations.action: File the annual report with the Florida Division of Corporations (Sunbiz) and pay the fee ($500).
obligations.penalty: $400 late fee after May 1
obligations.explanation: Florida requires every limited partnership or LLP registered in the state to file an annual report with the Florida Division of Corporations (Sunbiz) by May 1 each year. The fee is $500. Miss it and the result is $400 late fee after May 1. A company registered in more than one state files this in each of them. A general partnership that never registered with the state files no annual report in most states; the line is for limited partnerships and LLPs.

obligations.name: Florida nonprofit annual report
obligations.action: File the annual report with the Florida Division of Corporations (Sunbiz) and pay the fee ($61.25).
obligations.penalty: Administrative dissolution in September; nonprofits owe no late fee
obligations.explanation: A Florida nonprofit corporation files its annual report on Sunbiz between January 1 and May 1. The fee is $61.25. Nonprofits are spared the $400 late fee, but an entity that has not filed by the third Friday in September is dissolved.

obligations.name: Florida solicitation of contributions registration renewal
obligations.agency: Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services
obligations.action: Renew the registration with the Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services on the anniversary of the initial registration, with the Form 990 or the financial statement.
obligations.fee: $10 to $400, by contributions
obligations.penalty: $25 a month late; administrative fines up to $5,000 for soliciting unregistered
obligations.explanation: A charity that solicits in Florida registers with the Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services and renews every year on the anniversary of its first registration, so the date is the charity's own. The fee runs from $10 for contributions under $5,000 to $400 above $10 million. The Department sends a renewal notice; a late renewal costs $25 a month. Charities raising under $50,000 a year use a simplified registration with no fee; religious organizations and schools are exempt.

obligations.name: Florida corporate income tax return
obligations.action: File the Florida corporate income tax return with the Florida Department of Revenue by the 1st day of the 5th month after the fiscal year ends (May 1 for a calendar year) and pay any tax due. Most states follow the federal extension if one is filed.
obligations.explanation: Florida taxes corporate income, so a C corporation doing business there files a state return with the Florida Department of Revenue by the 1st day of the 5th month after the fiscal year ends (May 1 for a calendar year), later than the federal Form 1120. The state usually honors a federal extension to file, but not to pay. The form name and any minimum tax are on the state's site. Florida has no personal income tax, so an S corporation, partnership or LLC taxed as one files no Florida income tax return; an S corporation files Form F-1120 only in a year it owes federal tax.

obligations.explanation: A business that collects Florida sales tax files returns on a schedule the Florida Department of Revenue assigns from its volume: monthly for larger sellers, quarterly for most small ones, annually for the smallest. obligations.name: Georgia annual registration
obligations.action: File the annual registration with the Georgia Secretary of State and pay the fee: $50 plus a $10 online service charge ($60).
obligations.fee: $50 plus a $10 online service charge ($60)
obligations.penalty: $25 late fee; administrative dissolution after 60 days
obligations.explanation: Georgia requires every corporation registered in the state to file an annual registration with the Georgia Secretary of State by April 1 each year. A company registered in more than one state files this in each of them.

obligations.name: Georgia charitable organization registration renewal
obligations.agency: Georgia Secretary of State, Charities Division
obligations.action: Renew the charitable organization registration with the Secretary of State every two years, before it expires, with the most recent Form 990 and financial statement.
obligations.penalty: Expiration and a fine for soliciting while expired
obligations.explanation: A charity that solicits in Georgia registers with the Secretary of State and renews every two years, tied to the date of its first registration, so the date is the charity's own. The renewal fee is $20. Religious organizations, schools and charities raising under $25,000 a year are exempt.

The annual return is due even when the periodic returns paid everything.

obligations.action: File the Hawaii corporate income tax return with the Hawaii Department of Taxation by the 20th day of the 4th month after the fiscal year ends (April 20 for a calendar year) and pay any tax due. Most states follow the federal extension if one is filed.
obligations.explanation: Hawaii taxes corporate income, so a C corporation doing business there files a state return with the Hawaii Department of Taxation by the 20th day of the 4th month after the fiscal year ends (April 20 for a calendar year), later than the federal Form 1120. The state usually honors a federal extension to file, but not to pay. The form name and any minimum tax are on the state's site.

obligations.name: Hawaii corporate estimated tax payment
obligations.form: The state's estimated tax voucher or online payment

obligations.name: Nebraska unemployment insurance wage report

obligations.name: Nebraska annual withholding reconciliation

obligations.name: Nebraska sales tax return

obligations.explanation: A business that collects Nebraska sales tax files returns on a schedule the Nebraska Department of Revenue assigns from its volume: monthly for larger sellers, quarterly for most small ones, annually for the smallest. obligations.penalty: $75 late fee on the list and $100 on the license; default status after continued failure
obligations.explanation: A Nevada corporation files its annual list of officers and directors and renews its state business license by the last day of its anniversary month. The list costs $150 and the business license $500 for corporations. Nevada has no corporate or personal income tax, but it does have the Commerce Tax for businesses with over $4 million in Nevada revenue.

obligations.name: Nevada annual list and state business license
obligations.action: File the annual list and state business license with the Nevada Secretary of State and pay the fee ($150 annual list plus $200 state business license).

obligations.name: Nevada nonprofit annual list of officers
obligations.action: File the annual list of officers with the Nevada Secretary of State and pay the fee: $50; a 501(c) organization is exempt from the state business license.

obligations.penalty: $75 late fee; default status after continued failure
obligations.explanation: A Nevada nonprofit corporation files its annual list of officers and directors by the last day of its anniversary month. The fee is $50. An organization with a federal exemption under section 501(c) is exempt from the state business license and its fee; the charitable solicitation registration statement is filed with the same list.

obligations.penalty: Up to 10% of the tax plus interest
obligations.explanation: Nevada has no income tax; employers pay a payroll tax instead, the modified business tax, on wages above $50,000 a quarter, less what the employer paid for employee health care. It is filed quarterly by the last day of the month after the quarter, the same day as the unemployment report, and a return is due even when the wages are under the threshold. A payroll provider usually files it.

obligations.name: Nevada Commerce Tax return (Nevada revenue over $4 million)
obligations.action: File the Commerce Tax return for the fiscal year ending June 30 if Nevada gross revenue exceeded $4 million.

obligations.penalty: Up to 10% penalty plus interest
obligations.explanation: Nevada's Commerce Tax applies to businesses with more than $4 million in Nevada gross revenue in the fiscal year ending June 30. The return is due 45 days later, August 14. Businesses under the threshold no longer have to file. The line is shown from the $1 million revenue band so a growing company sees it coming; below $4 million there is nothing to do.

obligations.name: Nevada unemployment insurance wage report

obligations.name: New York charities annual filing
obligations.agency: New York Attorney General, Charities Bureau
obligations.action: File Form CHAR500 with the Form 990 and the fees four and a half months after the fiscal year ends, or with the IRS extension; a review is required above $250,000 in revenue and an audit above $1 million.
obligations.fee: $25 under Article 7-A plus $25 to $1,500 under the EPTL, by net worth
obligations.penalty: $1,000 per violation and cancellation of the registration
obligations.explanation: A charity that solicits or holds assets in New York registers with the Attorney General's Charities Bureau and files Form CHAR500 every year four and a half months after its fiscal year ends, May 15 for a calendar year, with the same extension as the Form 990. Two fees apply: $25 under Article 7-A for soliciting, and $25 to $1,500 under the Estates, Powers and Trusts Law by net worth. Revenue over $250,000 requires reviewed statements and over $1 million an audit. Religious organizations are exempt.

obligations.name: New York LLC annual filing fee
obligations.agency: New York State Department of Taxation and Finance
obligations.action: File Form IT-204-LL and pay the annual filing fee based on New York source gross income.
obligations.fee: $25 to $4,500 depending on New York source income
obligations.penalty: $50 a month late up to $1,500, plus interest
obligations.explanation: Every LLC and LLP with New York source income pays an annual filing fee on Form IT-204-LL by the 15th day of the third month after the year ends, March 15 for a calendar year. It runs from $25 for income under $100,000 to $4,500 above $25 million. It is separate from the biennial statement with the Department of State.

obligations.name: New York LLC beneficial ownership disclosure (status unsettled)
obligations.action: Check the Department of State's page before the deadline. If the filing portal is open, file the beneficial ownership disclosure, or an attestation of exemption; LLCs formed after January 1, 2026 file within 30 days of formation.
obligations.fee: Fee set by the Department of State; none published as of this check
obligations.penalty: Up to $500 a day for a disclosure more than 30 days late; suspension after two years
obligations.explanation: New York's LLC Transparency Act took effect January 1, 2026 and gives LLCs that existed before then until January 1, 2027 to disclose their beneficial owners to the Department of State or attest that an exemption applies. Its status is unsettled: the law takes its definitions from the federal Corporate Transparency Act, which now exempts US formed companies, the Governor vetoed a clarifying bill in December 2025, and as of this check the Department of State had published no form, portal or fee. The date stays on the calendar so nobody is caught out if the portal opens; Jay's monthly review tracks it, and the line will be withdrawn if the requirement lapses.

obligations.name: New York corporate income tax return
obligations.agency: New York State Department of Taxation and Finance
obligations.action: File the New York corporate income tax return with the New York State Department of Taxation and Finance by the 15th day of the 4th month after the fiscal year ends (April 15 for a calendar year) and pay any tax due. Most states follow the federal extension if one is filed.
obligations.explanation: New York taxes corporate income, so a C corporation doing business there files a state return with the New York State Department of Taxation and Finance by the 15th day of the 4th month after the fiscal year ends (April 15 for a calendar year), the same day as the federal Form 1120. The state usually honors a federal extension to file, but not to pay. The form name and any minimum tax are on the state's site.

obligations.name: New York corporate estimated tax payment
obligations.agency: New York State Department of Taxation and Finance
obligations.action: Pay the New York corporate estimated tax installment if the year's state tax will pass the state's threshold.
obligations.penalty: Underpayment interest, and in some states a penalty, on each short installment
obligations.explanation: Like the IRS, New York collects corporate income tax during the year once the expected tax passes a threshold the state sets (a few hundred to a thousand dollars in most states). Shown for every C corporation because the threshold is low; a corporation expecting no state tax can mark the lines handled.

obligations.name: New York pass through entity return
obligations.agency: New York State Department of Taxation and Finance
obligations.action: File the New York pass through entity return with the New York State Department of Taxation and Finance by the 15th day of the 3rd month after the fiscal year ends (March 15 for a calendar year), with the owners' state K-1s.
obligations.explanation: An S corporation or partnership doing business in New York files a state information return by the 15th day of the 3rd month after the fiscal year ends (March 15 for a calendar year), alongside the federal return, so the owners can report their shares on their own New York returns. Some states charge a minimum tax or filing fee with it; check the New York State Department of Taxation and Finance page.

obligations.name: New York personal income tax return with business income

obligations.explanation: An employer registers for unemployment insurance in each state where it has employees and files a wage report every quarter, by the last day of the month after the quarter in nearly every state: April 30, July 31, October 31 and January 31. The contribution rate is set by the state each year. Paying on time also earns the 5.4% credit against the federal unemployment tax.

obligations.name: New York fourth quarter withholding return with the annual wage totals

obligations.explanation: New York has no separate annual reconciliation form. The fourth quarter NYS-45, due January 31, carries each employee's annual wage and withholding totals and closes the year. Withholding payments during the year follow the schedule set by the employer's size, as often as within three business days of each payday. A payroll provider files it.

obligations.name: New York disability and paid family leave insurance
obligations.action: Withhold and remit the contributions through payroll, or keep the policy in force, as the program requires; there is no separate return.
obligations.explanation: New York requires every employer to carry disability benefits and paid family leave insurance, usually one policy from a private carrier or the State Insurance Fund, funded by an employee deduction capped each year. The obligation is the policy, not a filing; add its renewal date as your own date.

The date here is a planning reminder at the start of the year; the legal timing runs from each employee's hire date and the last training.

obligations.name: New York retirement savings mandate (New York Secure Choice, 10 or more employees)

obligations.action: Register with New York Secure Choice if the company has 10 or more employees in New York and no retirement plan of its own, then run the employee deductions through payroll; or certify that the company has its own plan.
obligations.penalty: Per employee penalties after notice, set by the state
obligations.explanation: New York requires an employer with no retirement plan of its own to enroll its employees in the state program, New York Secure Choice, which runs Roth IRAs funded by payroll deductions. The employer registers, uploads its employees and passes the deductions through; it contributes nothing and the employees can opt out. An employer that sponsors a 401(k), SIMPLE IRA or other plan certifies its exemption instead. Employers with ten or more New York employees in business for two years or more; registration windows ran from March to July 2026 by employer size, and a company past its window registers now. Registration deadlines have passed for existing employers, so a company not yet registered should register now; a new employer registers within the program's window after its first hire.

obligations.name: Ohio charitable organization annual report
obligations.agency: Ohio Attorney General, Charitable Law Section
obligations.action: File the annual report with the Attorney General online four and a half months after the fiscal year ends, with the Form 990 and the fees; the IRS extension carries over.
obligations.fee: Two fee schedules, by assets ($0 under $25,000, then $50, $100, $200) and by contributions ($0 under $5,000, then $50, $100, $200); a charity can owe both
obligations.penalty: $200 late fee and loss of registration
obligations.explanation: A charity formed in Ohio, holding assets there or soliciting there registers with the Attorney General's Charitable Law Section and files an annual report four and a half months after its fiscal year ends, May 15 for a calendar year, or later with the IRS extension. Two fee schedules apply and both can be owed: one by assets under the Charitable Trust Act (nothing under $25,000, then $50, $100 and $200 from $500,000) and one by contributions under the Charitable Organizations Act (nothing under $5,000, then $50, $100 from $25,000 and $200 from $50,000). Ohio has no exemption for small charities; religious organizations, schools and a few other categories are exempt and request the exemption online.

obligations.penalty: Up to 10% of the tax
obligations.explanation: Ohio has no corporate income tax and no annual report for corporations or LLCs. Businesses with more than $6 million in Ohio gross receipts pay the commercial activity tax instead, with quarterly returns due on the 10th day of the second month after each quarter. Below the threshold there is nothing to file; the line is shown from the $5 million revenue band.

obligations.fee: The premium adjustment for the policy year, by class code and actual payroll
obligations.penalty: Loss of the policy's rebates and discounts, and a lapsed policy after continued failure
obligations.explanation: Ohio is one of four states where employers buy workers' compensation from the state fund rather than an insurer. The Bureau estimates the premium for each policy year, July 1 to June 30, bills it in installments, and asks every employer to true up the estimate against actual payroll by August 15. Missing the true-up costs the policy its discounts and, if it continues, the coverage. Payroll providers do not file this one.

obligations.explanation: A charity that solicits in South Carolina registers with the Secretary of State and renews every year four and a half months after its fiscal year ends, May 15 for a calendar year, with the annual financial report. The fee is $50 and the late fee $10 a day. Religious organizations, schools and charities raising under $7,500 a year are exempt but file a registration exemption.

obligations.name: South Carolina corporate estimated tax payment
obligations.form: The state's estimated tax voucher or online payment
obligations.action: Pay the South Carolina corporate estimated tax installment if the year's state tax will pass the state's threshold.
obligations.penalty: Underpayment interest, and in some states a penalty, on each short installment
obligations.explanation: Like the IRS, South Carolina collects corporate income tax during the year once the expected tax passes a threshold the state sets (a few hundred to a thousand dollars in most states). The installments fall on the 15th day of the fourth, sixth, ninth and twelfth months of the fiscal year in most states, the same days as the federal ones; the South Carolina Department of Revenue page has the threshold and any state that differs. obligations.name: South Carolina pass through entity return
obligations.action: File the South Carolina pass through entity return with the South Carolina Department of Revenue by the 15th day of the 3rd month after the fiscal year ends (March 15 for a calendar year), with the owners' state K-1s.
obligations.explanation: An S corporation or partnership doing business in South Carolina files a state information return by the 15th day of the 3rd month after the fiscal year ends (March 15 for a calendar year), alongside the federal return, so the owners can report their shares on their own South Carolina returns. Some states charge a minimum tax or filing fee with it; check the South Carolina Department of Revenue page. The annual report and its $25 license fee travel with the return: Form SC1120 for a C corporation, SC1120S for an S corporation.

obligations.name: South Carolina personal income tax return with business income
obligations.action: Report the business income on the owner's South Carolina personal return by April 15 each year.
obligations.explanation: A sole proprietorship or single member LLC reports its income on the owner's South Carolina personal return, due April 15 each year in step with the federal Form 1040.

obligations.name: South Carolina unemployment insurance wage report
obligations.action: File the quarterly wage report and pay state unemployment insurance contributions for employees working in South Carolina.
obligations.penalty: Late filing and payment penalties set by the state, plus loss of the federal FUTA credit if contributions are not paid on time
obligations.explanation: An employer registers for unemployment insurance in each state where it has employees and files a wage report every quarter, by the last day of the month after the quarter in nearly every state: April 30, July 31, October 31 and January 31. The contribution rate is set by the state each year. Paying on time also earns the 5.4% credit against the federal unemployment tax.

obligations.name: South Carolina annual withholding reconciliation
obligations.action: File the annual reconciliation of South Carolina income tax withheld, with copies of the W-2s, and keep withholding deposits on the schedule the state assigned.
obligations.explanation: South Carolina withholds state income tax from employee wages, and the employer reconciles the year's withholding with the South Carolina Department of Revenue after year end, by January 31 in most states and the end of February in a few, with copies of the W-2s where the state takes them. Withholding deposits during the year follow a schedule the state assigns, monthly or quarterly for most small employers. A payroll provider normally handles both.

obligations.name: South Carolina sales tax return

obligations.explanation: A business that collects South Carolina sales tax files returns on a schedule the South Carolina Department of Revenue assigns from its volume: monthly for larger sellers, quarterly for most small ones, annually for the smallest. obligations.penalty: $25 a month late and expiration of the registration

obligations.name: Tennessee franchise and excise tax return

Some family owned and farming LLCs can apply for exemption; most operating businesses pay it.

obligations.fee: No tax below the no tax due threshold, $2,650,000 in annualized revenue for 2026 and 2027 (indexed every two years); 0.375% or 0.75% of margin above it
obligations.penalty: $50 late filing penalty plus 5% of the tax, rising to 10% after 30 days; forfeiture of the right to do business after continued failure
obligations.explanation: Texas has no corporate income tax and no annual report with the Secretary of State. Instead every taxable entity files with the Comptroller by May 15: a Public Information Report, and a franchise tax report if annualized revenue is above the no tax due threshold, $2,650,000 for the 2026 and 2027 reports and indexed every two years. Since 2024, entities below the threshold file only the Public Information Report. Forgetting the report costs $50 even when no tax is due, and an entity that stays delinquent loses its right to do business in Texas.

obligations.explanation: An S corporation or partnership doing business in Vermont files a state information return by the 15th day of the 3rd month after the fiscal year ends (March 15 for a calendar year), alongside the federal return, so the owners can report their shares on their own Vermont returns. Some states charge a minimum tax or filing fee with it; check the Vermont Department of Taxes page.

obligations.name: Vermont personal income tax return with business income
obligations.action: Report the business income on the owner's Vermont personal return by April 15 each year.
obligations.explanation: A sole proprietorship or single member LLC reports its income on the owner's Vermont personal return, due April 15 each year in step with the federal Form 1040.

obligations.name: Vermont unemployment insurance wage report
obligations.action: File the quarterly wage report and pay state unemployment insurance contributions for employees working in Vermont.
obligations.penalty: Late filing and payment penalties set by the state, plus loss of the federal FUTA credit if contributions are not paid on time
obligations.explanation: An employer registers for unemployment insurance in each state where it has employees and files a wage report every quarter, by the last day of the month after the quarter in nearly every state: April 30, July 31, October 31 and January 31. The contribution rate is set by the state each year. Paying on time also earns the 5.4% credit against the federal unemployment tax.

obligations.name: Vermont annual withholding reconciliation
obligations.action: File the annual reconciliation of Vermont income tax withheld, with copies of the W-2s, and keep withholding deposits on the schedule the state assigned.
obligations.explanation: Vermont withholds state income tax from employee wages, and the employer reconciles the year's withholding with the Vermont Department of Taxes after year end, by January 31 in most states and the end of February in a few, with copies of the W-2s where the state takes them. Withholding deposits during the year follow a schedule the state assigns, monthly or quarterly for most small employers. A payroll provider normally handles both.

obligations.name: Vermont retirement savings mandate (VT Saves, 5 or more employees)
obligations.form: Registration with the state program, then payroll deductions
obligations.action: Register with VT Saves if the company has 5 or more employees in Vermont and no retirement plan of its own, then run the employee deductions through payroll; or certify that the company has its own plan.
obligations.penalty: Per employee penalties after notice, set by the state
obligations.explanation: Vermont requires an employer with no retirement plan of its own to enroll its employees in the state program, VT Saves, which runs Roth IRAs funded by payroll deductions. The employer registers, uploads its employees and passes the deductions through; it contributes nothing and the employees can opt out. An employer that sponsors a 401(k), SIMPLE IRA or other plan certifies its exemption instead. Employers with five or more employees registered during 2026, and the 2026 amendments reach employers with as few as two; the penalty is $75 per eligible employee from October 2026. Registration deadlines have passed for existing employers, so a company not yet registered should register now; a new employer registers within the program's window after its first hire.

obligations.name: Vermont sales tax return
obligations.action: File the Vermont sales tax return and remit the tax collected, on the monthly, quarterly or annual schedule the state assigned.
obligations.penalty: Late filing and payment penalties plus interest; personal liability for the owners for tax collected and not remitted
obligations.explanation: A business that collects Vermont sales tax files returns on a schedule the Vermont Department of Taxes assigns from its volume: monthly for larger sellers, quarterly for most small ones, annually for the smallest. Dates here assume quarterly, due the 20th of the month after the quarter. Sales tax collected belongs to the state, and owners can be held personally liable for it.

obligations.name: Virginia annual report and registration fee
obligations.action: File the annual report and registration fee with the Virginia State Corporation Commission and pay the fee ($100 registration fee for up to 5,000 authorized shares, rising with share count).
obligations.fee: $100 registration fee for up to 5,000 authorized shares, rising with share count
obligations.penalty: $10 or 10% of the fee, whichever is greater; termination after continued failure
obligations.explanation: A Virginia corporation files an annual report and pays an annual registration fee to the State Corporation Commission by the last day of its anniversary month. The fee starts at $100 and rises with the number of authorized shares.

obligations.name: Virginia annual registration fee
obligations.action: File the annual registration fee with the Virginia State Corporation Commission and pay the fee ($50).
obligations.penalty: $25 late fee; cancellation after continued failure
obligations.explanation: A Virginia LLC pays a $50 annual registration fee to the State Corporation Commission by the last day of its anniversary month. There is no report to file, only the fee, which is easy to forget for exactly that reason.

obligations.name: Virginia annual registration fee
obligations.action: File the annual registration fee with the Virginia State Corporation Commission and pay the fee ($50).
obligations.penalty: $25 late fee; cancellation after continued failure
obligations.explanation: A Virginia LLC pays a $50 annual registration fee to the State Corporation Commission by the last day of its anniversary month. obligations.name: Virginia nonprofit annual report and registration fee
obligations.action: File the annual report and registration fee with the Virginia State Corporation Commission and pay the fee ($25).
obligations.penalty: $10 late fee; termination after continued failure
obligations.explanation: A Virginia nonstock corporation files an annual report and pays a $25 registration fee to the State Corporation Commission by the last day of its anniversary month.

obligations.name: Virginia charitable organization registration renewal
obligations.agency: Virginia Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services, Office of Charitable and Regulatory Programs
obligations.action: Renew the registration with the Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services on Form 102 by the 15th day of the fifth month after the fiscal year ends, with the Form 990, or request an extension before the date.
obligations.fee: $30 to $325, by contributions
obligations.penalty: $100 late fee and civil penalties for soliciting while unregistered
obligations.explanation: A charity that solicits in Virginia registers with the Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services and renews every year by the 15th day of the fifth month after its fiscal year ends, May 15 for a calendar year, the same day as the Form 990. The fee runs from $30 to $325 by contributions. Religious organizations, schools, hospitals and charities raising under $5,000 a year are exempt; several other categories file for an exemption rather than registering.

obligations.name: Virginia corporate income tax return
obligations.action: File the Virginia corporate income tax return with the Virginia Department of Taxation by the 15th day of the 4th month after the fiscal year ends (April 15 for a calendar year) and pay any tax due. Most states follow the federal extension if one is filed.
obligations.explanation: Virginia taxes corporate income, so a C corporation doing business there files a state return with the Virginia Department of Taxation by the 15th day of the 4th month after the fiscal year ends (April 15 for a calendar year), the same day as the federal Form 1120. The state usually honors a federal extension to file, but not to pay. The form name and any minimum tax are on the state's site.

obligations.name: Virginia corporate estimated tax payment
obligations.form: The state's estimated tax voucher or online payment
obligations.action: Pay the Virginia corporate estimated tax installment if the year's state tax will pass the state's threshold.
obligations.penalty: Underpayment interest, and in some states a penalty, on each short installment
obligations.explanation: Like the IRS, Virginia collects corporate income tax during the year once the expected tax passes a threshold the state sets (a few hundred to a thousand dollars in most states). The installments fall on the 15th day of the fourth, sixth, ninth and twelfth months of the fiscal year in most states, the same days as the federal ones; the Virginia Department of Taxation page has the threshold and any state that differs. Shown for every C corporation because the threshold is low; a corporation expecting no state tax can mark the lines handled.

obligations.name: Washington annual report
obligations.action: File the annual report with the Washington Secretary of State and pay the fee ($70).
obligations.penalty: $25 late fee; administrative dissolution after continued failure
obligations.explanation: Washington requires every corporation registered in the state to file an annual report with the Washington Secretary of State by the last day of the anniversary month of its formation. The fee is $70. Miss it and the result is $25 late fee; administrative dissolution after continued failure. A company registered in more than one state files this in each of them.

obligations.action: File the annual report with the Washington Secretary of State and pay the fee: $20 ($60 when gross revenue is $500,000 or more).
obligations.fee: $20 ($60 when gross revenue is $500,000 or more)
obligations.penalty: $25 late fee; administrative dissolution after continued failure
obligations.explanation: A Washington nonprofit corporation files its annual report by the last day of its anniversary month, up to 180 days early. The fee is $20, or $60 once gross revenue reaches $500,000.

obligations.penalty: $50 late fee and expiration of the registration
obligations.explanation: A charity that solicits in Washington registers with the Secretary of State's Charities Program and renews every year by the end of the eleventh month after its fiscal year ends, November 30 for a calendar year. The renewal fee is $40. Charities raising under $50,000 a year with no paid staff, religious organizations and political organizations are exempt but may register voluntarily.

obligations.name: Washington business and occupation tax return
obligations.action: File the combined excise tax return on the schedule the Department of Revenue assigned: monthly, quarterly or annually.
obligations.fee: Tax on gross receipts at a rate set by activity; small businesses get a credit that can reduce it to zero
obligations.penalty: 9% late penalty, rising to 29%
obligations.explanation: Washington has no income tax. Businesses pay a business and occupation tax on gross receipts instead, filed on the Department of Revenue's combined excise tax return. The Department assigns a monthly, quarterly or annual schedule; quarterly returns are due by the last day of the month after the quarter and annual returns by April 15. Dates here assume quarterly. A nonprofit owes the tax on business income only: contributions, grants and qualifying fundraising income are not taxed, and a nonprofit with no business income may have nothing to file.

obligations.name: Washington workers' compensation premium report
obligations.agency: Washington Department of Labor and Industries
obligations.action: File the quarterly workers' compensation report with Labor and Industries and pay the premium by the last day of the month after the quarter, the same day as the unemployment report.
obligations.fee: Premium by risk class and hours worked, part of it withheld from employees
obligations.penalty: Late filing penalties and interest; an employer that stops reporting loses coverage
obligations.explanation: Washington employers buy workers' compensation from the state fund, run by the Department of Labor and Industries, and report hours and pay the premium every quarter: April 30, July 31, October 31 and January 31. The report is separate from the unemployment wage report, though due the same day, and a payroll provider usually files both.

obligations.penalty: Interest and late penalties set by the program on premiums paid late
obligations.explanation: Washington's Paid Family and Medical Leave and WA Cares Fund premiums are a percentage of wages set each year, split between employer and employee (employers with fewer than 50 employees pay no employer share of Paid Leave), and reported every quarter to the Employment Security Department on a report of its own. The rate is set by the program each year, so the figure on the agency page is the one to use, and a payroll provider normally files the report.

obligations.name: West Virginia charitable organization registration renewal
obligations.action: Renew the charitable organization registration with the Secretary of State on the anniversary of the initial registration, with the Form 990; an audit is required above $500,000 in contributions.

obligations.penalty: Expiration and civil penalties for soliciting while expired
obligations.explanation: A charity that solicits in West Virginia registers with the Secretary of State and renews every year on the anniversary of its first registration, so the date is the charity's own. The fee is $15, or $50 once contributions pass $1 million. Religious organizations, schools, hospitals and charities raising under $50,000 a year with no paid fundraisers are exempt.

obligations.penalty: Administrative dissolution after one year of failure
obligations.explanation: A Wisconsin corporation files its annual report with the Department of Financial Institutions by the end of the calendar quarter in which it was incorporated. The fee is $25.

Religious organizations, schools and charities raising under $25,000 a year are exempt.

obligations.fee: No fee
obligations.penalty: Loss of the credential

obligations.name: Wisconsin annual withholding reconciliation
obligations.action: File the annual reconciliation of Wisconsin income tax withheld, with copies of the W-2s, and keep withholding deposits on the schedule the state assigned.
obligations.explanation: Wisconsin withholds state income tax from employee wages, and the employer reconciles the year's withholding with the Wisconsin Department of Revenue after year end, by January 31 in most states and the end of February in a few, with copies of the W-2s where the state takes them. Withholding deposits during the year follow a schedule the state assigns, monthly or quarterly for most small employers. A payroll provider normally handles both.

obligations.name: Wisconsin sales tax return
obligations.action: File the Wisconsin sales tax return and remit the tax collected, on the monthly, quarterly or annual schedule the state assigned.
obligations.penalty: Late filing and payment penalties plus interest; personal liability for the owners for tax collected and not remitted
obligations.explanation: A business that collects Wisconsin sales tax files returns on a schedule the Wisconsin Department of Revenue assigns from its volume: monthly for larger sellers, quarterly for most small ones, annually for the smallest. Dates here assume quarterly, due the last day of the month after the quarter. Sales tax collected belongs to the state, and owners can be held personally liable for it.

obligations.name: Wyoming annual report and license tax
obligations.action: File the annual report and license tax with the Wyoming Secretary of State and pay the fee ($60 minimum, or $0.0002 per dollar of assets located in Wyoming).
obligations.fee: $60 minimum, or $0.0002 per dollar of assets located in Wyoming
obligations.penalty: Administrative dissolution 60 days after the due date
obligations.explanation: A Wyoming corporation files its annual report and pays the license tax by the first day of its anniversary month. The tax is $60 or two tenths of a mill on Wyoming assets, whichever is greater. Wyoming has no corporate or personal income tax.

obligations.name: Wyoming annual report and license tax
obligations.action: File the annual report and license tax with the Wyoming Secretary of State and pay the fee ($60 minimum, or $0.0002 per dollar of assets located in Wyoming).
obligations.fee: $60 minimum, or $0.0002 per dollar of assets located in Wyoming
obligations.penalty: Administrative dissolution 60 days after the due date
obligations.explanation: Wyoming requires every LLC registered in the state to file an annual report and license tax with the Wyoming Secretary of State by the first day of the anniversary month of its formation. The fee is $60 minimum, or $0.0002 per dollar of assets located in Wyoming. Miss it and the result is administrative dissolution 60 days after the due date. A company registered in more than one state files this in each of them.

obligations.name: Wyoming annual report and license tax
obligations.action: File the annual report and license tax with the Wyoming Secretary of State and pay the fee ($60 minimum, or $0.0002 per dollar of assets located in Wyoming).
obligations.fee: $60 minimum, or $0.0002 per dollar of assets located in Wyoming
obligations.penalty: Administrative dissolution 60 days after the due date
obligations.explanation: Wyoming requires every limited partnership or LLP registered in the state to file an annual report and license tax with the Wyoming Secretary of State by the first day of the anniversary month of its formation. The fee is $60 minimum, or $0.0002 per dollar of assets located in Wyoming. Miss it and the result is administrative dissolution 60 days after the due date. A company registered in more than one state files this in each of them. A general partnership that never registered with the state files no annual report in most states; the line is for limited partnerships and LLPs.

obligations.name: Wyoming nonprofit annual report
obligations.action: File the annual report with the Wyoming Secretary of State and pay the fee ($25).
obligations.penalty: Administrative dissolution 60 days after the due date
obligations.explanation: A Wyoming nonprofit corporation files its annual report by the first day of its anniversary month. The fee is $25, with no license tax.

obligations.name: Wyoming charitable solicitation registration: not required
obligations.action: Nothing to file. Wyoming has no charitable solicitation registration.
obligations.explanation: Wyoming does not require charities to register before soliciting. A Wyoming nonprofit still files its annual report with the Secretary of State and its Form 990.

obligations.name: Wyoming unemployment insurance wage report
obligations.action: File the quarterly wage report and pay state unemployment insurance contributions for employees working in Wyoming.
obligations.penalty: Late filing and payment penalties set by the state, plus loss of the federal FUTA credit if contributions are not paid on time
obligations.explanation: An employer registers for unemployment insurance in each state where it has employees and files a wage report every quarter, by the last day of the month after the quarter in nearly every state: April 30, July 31, October 31 and January 31. The contribution rate is set by the state each year. Paying on time also earns the 5.4% credit against the federal unemployment tax. In Wyoming the workers' compensation premium is reported on the same quarterly filing.

obligations.name: Wyoming sales tax return
obligations.action: File the Wyoming sales tax return and remit the tax collected, on the monthly, quarterly or annual schedule the state assigned.
obligations.penalty: Late filing and payment penalties plus interest; personal liability for the owners for tax collected and not remitted
obligations.explanation: A business that collects Wyoming sales tax files returns on a schedule the Wyoming Department of Revenue assigns from its volume: monthly for larger sellers, quarterly for most small ones, annually for the smallest. Dates here assume quarterly, due the 20th of the month after the quarter. Sales tax collected belongs to the state, and owners can be held personally liable for it.

changes.title: Pre-launch review: paid leave, workers' compensation, state return dates, Delaware's $400 tax and the $2,000 1099 threshold
changes.summary: A review of the pack against what advisors expect on a small company's calendar added the employer programs the first pass lacked: paid family and medical leave premiums in the fourteen jurisdictions with a program (quarterly reports in Washington, Oregon, Massachusetts, Connecticut, Colorado, Delaware, Minnesota, Maine and DC, Maryland from 2027), the state fund workers' compensation filings in Ohio and Washington, the state retirement savings mandates, Massachusetts's HIRD, state corporate estimated taxes, California's minimum franchise tax, DC's business license and personal property return, Hawaii's annual general excise return and the summary annual report for retirement plans. Corrections: Delaware's LLC and partnership tax is $400 from the June 1, 2027 payment (House Bill 400) and a corporation formed elsewhere files Delaware's foreign report by June 30 at $250 rather than the March 1 franchise tax; the 1099-NEC threshold is $2,000 for 2026 payments; the partnership and S corporation late penalty is $255 a month; Texas's no tax due threshold is $2,650,000; Pennsylvania's charity renewal is November 15; Ohio's charity fees run on two schedules with no small charity exemption; state corporate returns fall on the state's own date in ten states (Florida May 1, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Oregon, Alaska and Louisiana May 15, Connecticut May 1, Michigan and Iowa April 30, Hawaii April 20) and pass through returns on April 15 in Illinois (partnerships), New Jersey and Pennsylvania. Logic: California's LLC tax, fee and Form 568 apply only to LLCs taxed as partnerships or disregarded entities, with the single member return on April 15; DC's franchise tax appears once; no sales tax return is generated for Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire or Oregon; a single member LLC with a nonresident owner sees the Form 1040-NR note instead of Schedule C.
changes.action: Read your calendar again after this release: a company with employees in a paid leave state, a Delaware company formed elsewhere, or a California LLC taxed as a corporation will see lines added, moved or removed.

changes.title: Nonprofits join the rules pack: Form 990 family, state nonprofit reports, charitable registration
changes.summary: The pack now covers nonprofit corporations. Federal: Form 990-N, 990-EZ, 990 and 990-PF by the 15th day of the fifth month after the fiscal year, Form 990-T for unrelated business income, donor acknowledgments by January 31, and the 501(c)(3) exemption from federal unemployment tax. Every state and the District of Columbia: the nonprofit corporation's own report where it differs from the business corporation's, and charitable solicitation registration in the 37 states and the District that require it, with a line for the states that do not. Also in this release: Colorado's periodic report fee, $25 since July 2024, and Utah's repeal of charitable registration in 2024.
changes.action: Nothing to file. A nonprofit that built a calendar before this release should rebuild it with the Nonprofit corporation entity to see the new lines.

changes.title: FinCEN permanently exempts US formed companies from beneficial ownership reporting
changes.summary: A final rule from the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, effective August 14, 2026, makes permanent the March 2025 exemption of domestic companies from the Corporate Transparency Act's beneficial ownership reporting. Corporations, LLCs and other entities formed by a filing with a US state no longer file a BOI report, and FinCEN is deleting the reports US companies filed earlier. Companies formed under foreign law and registered in a US state still report their non US owners. The federal rule does not displace state rules such as New York's LLC Transparency Act.
changes.action: Nothing to file. If a service provider is still charging you to prepare a federal BOI report, cancel it.

changes.title: New York LLC Transparency Act takes effect
changes.summary: New York now requires LLCs formed or registered in the state to file a beneficial ownership disclosure with the Department of State, or an attestation that an exemption applies. LLCs formed on or after January 1, 2026 file within 30 days of formation. LLCs that existed before that date have until January 1, 2027. The state requirement is independent of the federal exemption.
changes.action: New York LLCs: file the disclosure or exemption attestation before January 1, 2027.

changes.title: Pennsylvania begins requiring annual reports
changes.summary: For the first time, Pennsylvania business entities file an annual report with the Department of State: corporations by June 30, LLCs by September 30, and limited partnerships, LLPs and business trusts by December 31. The fee is $7. There is no penalty for reports missed in 2025 and 2026; from 2027, an entity that fails to file is administratively dissolved six months after its due date.
changes.action: Pennsylvania entities: add the report to the calendar now; the 2027 report is the first one with consequences.

changes.title: Oklahoma repeals the corporate franchise tax
changes.summary: Oklahoma's franchise tax on corporations no longer applies for tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2024. Corporations file no annual report with the Secretary of State either. Oklahoma LLCs still file their annual certificate on the anniversary of formation.

changes.title: Texas stops requiring No Tax Due franchise reports
changes.summary: For reports due in 2024 and later, a Texas entity with annualized revenue under the no tax due threshold files only its Public Information Report (or Ownership Information Report) by May 15. The separate No Tax Due Report is gone. Entities above the threshold still file the franchise tax report.

changes.title: Alabama exempts small entities from the business privilege tax
changes.summary: For tax years beginning after December 31, 2023, an Alabama entity whose business privilege tax would be $100 or less owes nothing and does not file the return. Alabama also stopped requiring a separate annual report with the Secretary of State for domestic entities.
